questions.answer: Do not let the team send a trade payment as a remittance; check the documentation, the screening, and the settlement requirements for each type, and show how sending a trade payment as a remittance can cause it to be held or rejected. Walk through a real payment and show which type it is, and what would happen if it was sent as the wrong type.
questions.question: A business user insists on sending a trade payment as a remittance to save money. How do you persuade them not to?

questions.answer: First check whether the payment was sent via the right correspondent chain and whether any bank in the chain deducted a charge. If a charge was deducted, explain that to the customer with the evidence. If no charge was deducted, check the FX rate and whether it moved between instruction and settlement.
questions.question: You are the BA when a customer says the beneficiary received less than expected, but no one can explain why. How do you trace the amount through the correspondent chain?

questions.answer: Explain that gpi tracking shows confirmations from banks in the chain, but it does not prove the money has been credited to the beneficiary account. Show the customer the gpi confirmations and the beneficiary bank's statement entry, and explain the stages between a confirmation and a credit. If the credit has not happened, use an investigation to ask the beneficiary bank for the status.
questions.question: A customer thinks gpi tracking proves their payment has been credited. How do you explain what gpi actually shows, and what it does not show?

questions.answer: Do not accept the de-risking decision without understanding the reason; check whether the bank stopped the service because of compliance risk, cost, or a lack of volume. Propose a review of the affected customers, and a process to help them find an alternative correspondent bank. Present the impact to the business, so they can decide whether to accept the de-risking or to find a way to continue the service.
questions.question: A bank has de-risked a country and customers can no longer send payments there. How do you help the business decide what to do for the affected customers?

questions.answer: Check the correspondent chain and whether any bank in the chain has a limit on the amount, the currency, or the value date. If the chain is long, explain that each bank adds time and cost, and check whether a direct correspondent could be used. Tell the customer the options, and do not promise a time you cannot control.
questions.question: You are the BA when a high-value cross-border payment is stuck at an intermediary bank and no one can tell you why. How do you investigate?

questions.answer: First confirm the charge instruction, the amount sent, and the amount received, and compare them against the intermediary charges. If an intermediary deducted a charge despite the OUR instruction, explain that to the customer and ask the intermediary why they deducted it. Tell the customer the options, including a different route or a different charge option.
questions.question: A customer chose SHA charges, but the beneficiary received much less than expected. How do you explain what happened?

questions.answer: Explain that FX conversion timing determines the rate that is applied, and that converting at instruction locks the rate, while converting at settlement means the rate can move. Show how a payment converted at settlement can result in a different amount than quoted, and agree a process to convert at instruction where possible. Tell the customer the risk if the conversion is not done at instruction.
questions.question: A stakeholder asks why it matters whether FX conversion happens at instruction or at settlement. How do you explain it with a real example?

questions.answer: Do not let the team route a payment through a sanctioned bank, even if it is the only route that is fast or cheap. Check the sanctions list for every bank in the chain, and if any is sanctioned, stop the payment and escalate to compliance. Tell the customer why the payment cannot go via that route, and offer an alternative route that is compliant.
questions.question: You are the BA when a proposed routing for a payment goes through a bank that is under sanctions. What do you do?

questions.answer: Check the nostro balance, the value date, and whether any incoming funds that were expected have not arrived. If the balance is short, ask treasury whether to fund the account or to delay the payment. Tell the customer the options and the impact, and do not promise a same-day payment if the nostro cannot be funded in time.
questions.question: A cross-border payment cannot be settled because the nostro account is short of funds in that currency. How do you handle it?

questions.answer: Explain that value dating determines when the beneficiary can use the funds, and that a payment with a future value date will not be available until that date. Show how a holiday in the beneficiary country can delay availability, and tell the customer the value date and the availability date. Check whether a different value date could have been used, and add a holiday check to the validation.
questions.question: A customer is angry because a payment they sent on Friday will not be available until Tuesday. How do you explain value dating and holidays?

questions.answer: First check the intermediary chain, the cut-off times, and whether any bank held the payment for screening. If the chain is long, explain that each bank adds time, and check whether a direct route could be used. Tell the customer what stage the payment reached, and give them a realistic timeline.
questions.question: You are the BA when a cross-border payment is delayed and the customer wants to know exactly where it is. How do you trace it through the correspondent chain?

questions.answer: Do not choose an intermediary based on cost alone; check the intermediary's cut-off, its screening process, and whether it has a direct relationship with the beneficiary bank. A cheaper intermediary that is slow may be worse than a more expensive one that is fast and reliable. Walk through a real payment and show which intermediary it should use.
questions.question: A team wants to use the cheapest intermediary bank for all cross-border payments. Why might that be a bad idea, and what would you propose instead?

questions.answer: Check the FX rate, the value date, and whether the payment was converted at instruction or at settlement. If the rate moved, explain that the amount received depends on the rate at settlement, unless a fixed rate was agreed. Agree a process to lock the rate at instruction where possible, and tell the customer the risk if the rate is not locked.
questions.question: A customer says they lost money because the FX rate moved after they instructed the payment. How do you explain the risk and what could have been done to avoid it?

questions.answer: First confirm whether the payment was held for sanctions screening, a compliance check, or a missing document. If it was held for screening, explain the process and the expected time, and do not promise a time you cannot control. If it was held for a missing document, ask the customer for the document and tell them what will happen once it is received.
questions.question: A cross-border payment has been held for three days and the customer is threatening to complain to the regulator. How do you handle the conversation and the investigation?

questions.answer: Explain that a remittance is typically a low-value, person-to-person payment, while a trade payment is a higher-value payment linked to a trade transaction. Show how the two have different documentation and screening requirements, and how sending a trade payment as a remittance can cause it to be held. Walk through a real payment and show which type it is.
questions.question: A business user is confused about the difference between a remittance payment and a trade payment. How do you explain it using a real example?

questions.answer: Check the currency cut-off, the value date, and whether the payment can be settled the next day. Tell the customer the new value date and any impact on charges, and check whether a different settlement system with a later cut-off could have been used. Add a cut-off check to the payment validation, so future payments are flagged before they miss the cut-off.
questions.question: You are the BA when a payment in a foreign currency misses its cut-off and the customer needed it today. What are your options?

questions.answer: Do not let the team assume gpi tracking means the payment has arrived; check whether the confirmation came from the final beneficiary bank or an intermediary. Ask for the beneficiary bank's statement entry and compare the reference, amount, and value date. If the credit went to a suspense account, raise it as an investigation.
questions.question: A payment shows as completed in gpi, but the beneficiary bank says it has no record of it. How do you resolve the discrepancy?

questions.answer: Specify that the system must store the original instruction, every intermediary confirmation, every FX rate applied, and every charge deducted, linked by a single trace ID. Require a single view that shows the full history in time order, so operations can trace a payment from instruction to credit. Test the view with a payment that was delayed, held for screening, and then credited, to prove the history is complete.
questions.question: You are asked to design the audit trail for cross-border payments in a new hub. What would you require so operations can trace a payment from instruction to final credit, including FX and charges?

questions.answer: Initiation only creates and validates the instruction, so the payment sits in a pending state while checks run. Next come fraud, sanctions, balance and limit checks, then authorisation to debit the account. Only after authorisation does execution begin, with clearing and settlement moving the funds to the beneficiary bank.
questions.question: A customer initiates a payment in the app and sees it as pending, but their balance has not changed. Walk through what has happened so far in the payment lifecycle and what still has to happen before the money leaves their account.

questions.answer: First check the payment status and reference in your own system, then confirm whether it was authorised, executed and sent to the rail or clearing system. Then check the rail status, any intermediary or beneficiary-bank hold, and the value date, since a payment can be sent but not yet due to be credited. Share the reference and the exact stage with the customer instead of guessing.
questions.question: A customer says they sent money yesterday and the recipient still has not received it. What steps do you trace, in order, to find where the payment is stuck?

questions.answer: Push back on treating the pending amount as final, because authorisation is only the issuer approving the purchase and placing a hold, and the final amount can legitimately change with a tip, currency conversion or adjustment. Clearing is the merchant presenting the final transaction, and settlement is when funds actually move between acquirer and issuer. Fix the customer messaging to show that the pending amount is a hold that can change, rather than changing the underlying process to hide it.
questions.question: You are the BA investigating complaints that card charges change between the pending amount and the final charge. A stakeholder insists the pending amount should be treated as final to stop the complaints. How do you explain what is really happening, and what do you change instead?

questions.answer: Use a real-time or high-value rail for the urgent supplier payment because speed and same-day value matter more than cost. Use a bulk credit-transfer file for payroll because it is efficient, predictable and can carry a future value date. Use a low-cost standard transfer or instant payment for the small refund, depending on how quickly the customer expects it.
questions.question: You have three payments to send: an urgent high-value supplier payment, monthly payroll for 200 staff, and a low-value refund to a customer. How do you choose the right rail for each, and why?

questions.answer: The payment should be marked failed for insufficient funds, not retried silently without a clear rule, and the customer should be notified promptly. Many banks retry once on a defined schedule or on the next working day, but the customer needs to know the payment did not go out and what will happen next. If it is a bill or loan payment, warn them about possible late fees from the payee.
questions.question: A standing instruction fails because there are insufficient funds. What should happen next, and what would you tell the customer?

questions.answer: The cancellation may not have reached the originator in time, or the mandate record was not updated before the collection file was created. First check the cancellation timestamp against the presentment date, then stop future collections and raise a refund or indemnity claim for the debit taken after cancellation. Tell the customer the debit will be returned and confirm the mandate is now closed.
questions.question: A customer cancels a direct debit mandate, but a debit is still presented the next day. What went wrong, and what do you do?

questions.answer: Check the agreed value date first, because the transaction date is when the instruction was made while the value date is when funds are treated as available and interest starts or stops running. If Monday was the agreed value date, the bank is correct even though the instruction was made on Friday. Explain this with the payment terms and the calendar, and suggest an earlier cut-off or a different rail next time if same-day value matters.
questions.question: A corporate treasurer disputes interest charged on a payment made on Friday but value-dated Monday, arguing the money left on Friday so interest should stop then. You are the BA asked to resolve the dispute. How do you decide who is right, and what do you tell the treasurer?

questions.answer: Reject the stakeholder's definition, because processing only means checks passed and the payment is on its way through the rail or clearing system. Pending means the instruction is received but not yet authorised or executed, settled means funds have reached the beneficiary bank, and failed means it was stopped or rejected and the money should be returned or never left. At the failed stage support must give a clear next step and a timescale, not just repeat the word failed.
questions.question: A stakeholder insists that a payment showing as processing means the money has already arrived, and wants support to tell customers that. You are the BA who has to define the statuses for the app. What definitions do you set, and what must support say at each stage?

questions.answer: Compare amount, beneficiary, value date, source channel and the unique instruction ID, not just the reference, because a customer reference can legitimately repeat. If the instruction IDs match, treat it as a duplicate and block the second submission. If they are separate instructions, process both but flag the pattern for the customer to confirm.
questions.question: Two payments are submitted with the same customer reference. How do you tell whether this is a genuine duplicate or two legitimate payments, and what do you do?

questions.answer: Once a credit transfer is executed, it usually cannot be pulled back unilaterally, so you start a recall request to the beneficiary bank and ask the beneficiary to consent to return the funds. If the payment is still pending or not yet executed, you may be able to stop it. Never promise the money will come back, because recovery depends on the receiving bank and the recipient.
questions.question: A customer sends money to the wrong account number and realises it ten minutes later. What are the realistic options, and what should you not promise?

questions.answer: The payment is normally held and executed on the next working day with the next available value date, unless an instant or alternative rail is available. Explain the cut-off clearly, offer the fastest valid alternative, and confirm the new expected date in writing. Record the missed cut-off as the cause so the case is not treated as a system failure.
questions.question: A high-value payment misses the cut-off on a Friday evening. What happens to it, and how do you handle the customer who needed it paid that day?

questions.answer: All channels must validate the beneficiary, amount, currency, value date, limits and sanctions screening before execution. An API or app can validate each field in real time and reject a bad instruction immediately, while a bulk file needs file-level checks plus item-level validation and a report of which items passed or failed. The business rules should be the same, even if the timing of the feedback differs.
questions.question: The same payment can be submitted through an API, a mobile app, or a bulk file upload. What validation should happen in each channel, and where do the checks differ?

questions.answer: Show the customer the mismatch and ask them to confirm the correct name and account details before proceeding, rather than auto-rejecting a small spelling difference. If they confirm, record their confirmation and proceed; if they are unsure, stop the payment and ask them to check with the beneficiary. This balances fraud prevention with a workable customer experience.
questions.question: A payment is flagged because the beneficiary name does not closely match the account name. How do you handle it without simply blocking every near match?

questions.answer: Follow the agreed prioritisation rules, which usually put time-critical, regulatory and customer-committed payments first, then process the rest in instruction order or by value date. Do not reorder payments arbitrarily, because that can breach a customer instruction or a contractual deadline. Tell the customer which payments are queued and what funding is needed to release them.
questions.question: Several payments are queued because the account does not have enough funds to cover them all. How do you decide which payments go first?

questions.answer: Split payments can confuse reconciliation because the supplier sees two amounts against one invoice reference, and they can look like an attempt to avoid a limit or control. Keep the same invoice reference on both parts, tell the supplier in advance, and record why the payment was split. If splitting is used to bypass a limit, escalate it instead of processing it.
questions.question: A supplier invoice is paid in two parts because the full amount would breach a daily limit. What risks does a split payment create, and how do you manage them?

questions.answer: Explain whether the rate was locked at initiation or applied at execution, and whether the customer or the beneficiary bears the conversion cost. If the rate was locked, show the locked rate and the amount sent; if it floated, explain that the final amount depends on the rate at execution. Always show fees and the exchange rate separately so the customer can see the breakdown.
questions.question: A customer sends money abroad and the amount received is less than expected because of a foreign exchange difference. How do you explain who bears the difference and when the rate is fixed?

questions.answer: Check the return reason first, because a wrong account number, closed account or missing information must be fixed before any retry. In most cases you create a new payment with corrected details rather than re-presenting the failed instruction, so the audit trail stays clear. Tell the customer why it was returned and confirm the corrected details before sending it again.
questions.question: A payment is returned by the beneficiary bank two days after it was sent. Do you re-present the same payment or create a new one, and what do you check first?

questions.answer: The agent treated two different instruments as the same: a standing instruction is set up by the payer, who controls the amount, date and cancellation, while a direct debit mandate authorises the payee to collect varying amounts, so the payer cancels the mandate with the bank and should also tell the payee. Fix the process so support first identifies which instrument it is, confirms the cancellation in the right system, and checks that no further collection is scheduled. Apologise, refund the collection taken after the request, and confirm the mandate is now closed.
questions.question: A customer asks support to stop a recurring payment, and the agent cancels a standing instruction when the payment was actually a direct debit mandate, so the next collection still goes out. You are the BA reviewing the incident. What went wrong, and what process fix do you propose?

questions.answer: The reference exceeded the field limit for that rail or message format and was truncated, so the beneficiary received only part of it. Check the field limits for each rail before sending, use a shorter structured reference where possible, and put the full invoice number in a remittance field or a separate advice. If truncation has already happened, send the beneficiary a remittance advice with the full reference.
questions.question: A payment reference is cut off because the field is too short, so the beneficiary cannot match the payment to an invoice. What went wrong and how do you prevent it?

questions.answer: Process the valid payments and reject only the failed item, unless the file has a control total or a regulatory rule that requires the whole file to balance. Tell the employer exactly which payment failed and why, so they can correct and resubmit just that item. Rejecting 199 good salary payments because of one error would cause far more harm than isolating the bad item.
questions.question: A bulk payroll file has 200 payments and one fails validation. Should you reject the whole file or process the other 199, and what do you tell the employer?

questions.answer: Do not resend it immediately, because the money may be sitting in a suspense or return account while the beneficiary bank decides, and a second payment could double-pay. First confirm the rejection reason and the exact location of the funds, then correct the fault, for example a closed account or missing detail, before sending a new payment. Tell the customer the funds are held safely, the reason for the rejection, and the new expected date.
questions.question: A payment was executed but the beneficiary bank rejects it, and operations wants to resend it straight away to keep the customer happy. You are the BA on the case. Where could the money be sitting, and why is an immediate resend risky?

questions.answer: Do not promise instant for every payment, because instant rails have limits, cut-offs and eligibility rules, and some payments must go by standard transfer. Offer the fastest rail that actually fits this payment, state the expected arrival time honestly, and explain the trade-off between speed, cost and limits. A missed promise damages trust far more than a clear next-working-day date given up front.
questions.question: A stakeholder insists support should promise instant payment for every transfer to reduce complaints. You are the BA who has to set the customer promise. When would you refuse to promise instant, and what do you offer instead?

questions.answer: Trace it in order: file received and validated, individual items authorised against funds and limits, file executed on the agreed value date, then clearing and settlement to each employee bank. If a payment is missing, check whether its item failed validation, the file was executed late, or the receiving bank has not yet credited it. Give the employer a per-employee status list, not a single file-level answer.
questions.question: An employer sends a salary file for 200 staff and three employees say they were not paid. You are the BA tracing the file. What do you check at each stage of the lifecycle, and what do you report back?

questions.answer: Explain that the hotel took an authorisation hold, not a second charge, and the hold will drop off after clearing or after the issuer releases it, which can take days. Show the customer the authorised amount, the final settled amount and the hold expiry, and do not promise an instant release unless the merchant has actually released it. If the hold is causing hardship, ask the merchant to release it and log the request.
questions.question: A customer stayed at a hotel, sees a hold on their card plus the final bill, and insists they have been charged twice. How do you investigate it, and what do you tell them about the authorisation hold?

questions.answer: Whether you can amend it depends on its status: a pending instruction can often be changed or cancelled, but once it is executed it usually cannot be edited and must be recalled or replaced. Check the status first, then tell operations what is possible for this specific payment rather than applying a blanket rule. If it cannot be changed, start a recall or a corrected new payment and record the original instruction for audit.
questions.question: Operations asks you to change the amount and beneficiary of a payment after it has been submitted. You are the BA asked whether this is possible. How do you decide, and what do you do if it is too late to amend?

questions.answer: Do not retry indefinitely, because repeated attempts can trigger fraud alerts, duplicate charges and customer complaints, and a mandate failure has a different fix from a card failure. Check the failure reason, for example expired card, insufficient funds or cancelled mandate, then retry once on a sensible schedule and notify the customer to update their details. If the mandate itself is cancelled, stop retrying and ask the customer to set up a new one.
questions.question: A recurring subscription payment fails and product wants the system to keep retrying it every day until it succeeds. You are the BA setting the retry policy. Why do you push back, and what retry rule do you propose instead?

questions.answer: Never resend blindly, because the original payment may have succeeded and a second submission would double-pay. Mark it as status unknown, check the rail, gateway and bank responses, and reconcile against the account before deciding. Only send a new payment once you have confirmed the original did not execute, and log the investigation so the duplicate risk is visible.
questions.question: A payment times out and the system shows its status as unknown, and operations wants to send it again immediately. You are the BA on the incident. Why is that dangerous, and what do you do first?

questions.answer: Explain that value dates follow working days and the receiving bank's calendar, so a Saturday instruction normally takes the next working day's value date even if the app accepts it on Saturday. Offer an instant rail if one is available and the amount qualifies, otherwise confirm the Monday value date in writing. Do not backdate the value date to meet the customer's expectation, as that would misstate interest and settlement.
questions.question: A treasurer submits a payment on Saturday and expects Saturday value dating, but the system gives Monday. You are the BA explaining the outcome. What do you tell them, and what alternative do you offer?

questions.answer: Prioritise by the agreed funding rules, usually regulatory, time-critical and customer-committed payments first, and do not send payments that would overdraw the nostro account. Alert treasury immediately with the shortfall, the queued payments and the funding needed, and tell affected customers the realistic revised timing. Sending payments without nostro cover risks rejects, fees and a failed settlement.
questions.question: Your nostro account does not have enough funds to cover all outbound cross-border payments due today. You are the BA in the morning funding meeting. How do you decide which payments go, and who do you alert?

questions.answer: First confirm the payment did arrive at the beneficiary bank and ask for its reference, amount, value date and sender details so the beneficiary can search their unallocated receipts. Then send a remittance advice with the full invoice number, and agree a process fix such as a mandatory structured reference or a shorter invoice code. Do not simply resend the payment, as that creates a duplicate.
questions.question: A supplier says a payment never arrived and threatens a late fee, but your bank shows it was settled. The payment had no invoice reference. You are the BA resolving it. How do you prove it arrived and help the supplier allocate it?

questions.answer: Support a risk-based step-up, not a blanket block or a frictionless pass: low-risk payments go straight through, while unusual amount, new beneficiary or high-risk corridor triggers an extra check. Explain to product that a short delay for a small number of payments prevents fraud losses that would cost far more in refunds and trust. Measure the false-positive rate and tune the rules, rather than turning the check off after the first complaint.
questions.question: Product wants payments to be completely frictionless, while risk wants every unusual payment blocked. You are the BA designing the fraud check. What compromise do you propose, and how do you justify it to both sides?

questions.answer: Start from the customer's claim and the mandate evidence: check whether a valid mandate existed, whether the amount and date matched it, and whether the customer was notified in advance. If the debit was outside the mandate or no mandate existed, process the indemnity refund promptly and recover from the originator. If the mandate was valid, explain the evidence to the customer and offer to cancel the mandate for the future.
questions.question: A customer claims a direct debit was unauthorised and demands an immediate refund under the indemnity. You are the BA handling the claim. What evidence do you check first, and when do you refund?

questions.answer: Explain that a bank cannot unilaterally reverse a completed credit transfer, because the funds now belong to the recipient's account and only the recipient or their bank can return them. Start a recall request, contact the beneficiary bank, and ask the customer to give the beneficiary's details to speed up consent. Set the expectation that recovery is not guaranteed and give a clear timeline for updates.
questions.question: A customer sent the wrong amount to a supplier and insists the bank should just reverse it. You are the BA explaining recall versus reversal. What can the bank actually do, and what should you not promise?

questions.answer: Do not choose the cheapest rail for every payment, because cost is only one factor alongside speed, value date, limits, tracking and the corridor's reliability. Use the low-cost rail for routine low-value payments where next-day arrival is fine, and a faster or high-value rail where the deadline or amount demands it. Show the stakeholder the cost of a late payment, such as penalties or lost supplier trust, against the small saving on fees.
questions.question: A stakeholder insists the cheapest rail should be used for all cross-border payments to save fees. You are the BA choosing rails for a mixed portfolio. When do you overrule the cheapest option, and how do you justify it?

questions.answer: Treat them differently, because a validation failure means the instruction never left the bank and the fix is in the data, while an execution failure means it left and may be in transit, held or returned. Give operations a different playbook for each: correct and resubmit for validation failures, trace and recall for execution failures. A single generic error message hides this distinction and leads to duplicate sends.
questions.question: Your developers want one generic error message for every failed payment to keep the code simple. You are the BA arguing for separate handling. Why must a failure at validation be treated differently from a failure at execution?

questions.answer: Be honest about the limit of visibility: once a payment leaves your bank it can sit with an intermediary or the beneficiary bank, and your system may only show that it was sent. Give the customer the reference, amount, value date and the last confirmed stage, then raise a trace with the intermediary and commit to an update time. Do not invent an arrival time you cannot verify.
questions.question: A payment is in transit with an intermediary bank and the customer wants an exact arrival time, but your system has no further tracking. You are the BA handling the complaint. What do you tell them, and what action do you take behind the scenes?

questions.answer: Check the change's effective date against the next due date: a change made the day before is often too late because the instruction was already created or the file was already sent. If the old amount will still go out, warn the customer, arrange a refund or adjustment for the difference, and confirm the new amount from the following cycle. Fix the app to show the effective date clearly before the customer confirms the change.
questions.question: A customer changes their standing order amount the day before it is due, but the old amount still goes out. They say the app let them change it, so it should have worked. You are the BA reviewing the case. What went wrong, and what do you fix?

questions.answer: Design logging at every stage, initiation, validation, authorisation, execution, clearing, settlement and return, with the instruction ID, timestamps, user, amounts and status changes. That trail lets an auditor follow one payment end to end without relying on anyone's memory. If a stage is missing from the logs, treat it as a control gap and add it, rather than asking operations to reconstruct it from emails.
questions.question: An auditor asks you to prove exactly what happened to a single payment from initiation to settlement. You are the BA designing the audit trail for a new payments system. What must be logged at each step, and why?

questions.answer: Compare the customer's claim with the authorisation evidence, such as the mandate, the signed instruction, the device and the timestamp, and check whether the amount and beneficiary match what was authorised. If the evidence shows a valid authorisation, explain it to the customer with the specific details and offer a dispute route with the payee. If the evidence is missing or inconsistent, treat it as an unauthorised payment and follow the refund and investigation process.
questions.question: A customer disputes a debit they say they never authorised, but the payee produces a signed instruction. You are the BA deciding the case. What evidence settles it, and what do you do if the evidence is inconclusive?

questions.answer: Escalate immediately with the facts: which payments are affected, how long they are delayed, the cause, and the revised timing. Offer the affected customers a proactive update and, where possible, an alternative rail, and log the breach against the SLA for the service review. Hiding the delay only turns a service failure into a trust failure when customers discover it themselves.
questions.question: A payment run breaches its service level and several business customers will miss their own deadlines. A stakeholder suggests saying nothing until the payments arrive. You are the BA on the incident. What do you do instead, and why?

questions.answer: Do not tell the merchant to simply retry the card, because a decline can mean insufficient funds, a fraud block, an expired card or a technical failure, and repeated attempts can lock the card. Check the decline reason code first, then ask the customer to try another payment method or contact their issuer. Log the reason code so the merchant can see whether this is a customer problem or a system problem.
questions.question: A customer's card is declined at a shop till and the merchant keeps retrying it, hoping it will go through. You are the BA called in after the card is blocked. What went wrong, and what should the merchant have done instead?

questions.answer: Push back on removing 3DS entirely, because it provides strong customer authentication and shifts liability for fraud away from the merchant in many cases. Instead, use risk-based 3DS so low-risk transactions pass with a frictionless check and only higher-risk ones get a challenge. Measure the abandonment rate by risk band, and fix the challenge experience, such as a broken app redirect, before blaming the check itself.
questions.question: A merchant's customers keep abandoning checkout when the 3DS challenge appears, and product wants to remove 3DS altogether. You are the BA weighing conversion against fraud. What do you recommend, and why?

questions.answer: Design the system to store a token, not the card number, and to update the token automatically when the card is replaced, so recurring payments continue without the customer re-entering details. If a token is not updated, the recurring payment fails and the customer must be asked to update their card. Never store the full card number to solve this, as that creates a PCI-DSS risk.
questions.question: A customer's card is replaced after it is lost, and all their recurring card payments start failing. You are the BA designing the fix. How should tokenisation have prevented this, and what do you do for customers already affected?

questions.answer: Explain that contactless has a per-transaction limit and a cumulative limit, after which a PIN is required as a security step-up, and that a high-value tap will therefore be declined for contactless. Ask the customer to insert the card and enter the PIN, which resets the contactless counter. Do not raise the limit for one customer on the spot, as the limit is a scheme and bank control.
questions.question: A customer tries to pay a large amount by tapping their card and it is declined, but the same card works when inserted with a PIN. They insist the card is faulty. You are the BA explaining the outcome. What is happening, and what do you tell them?

questions.answer: First check the reason code, because a fraud claim needs different evidence from a duplicate or goods-not-received claim. For fraud, the merchant needs proof of authentication, delivery and the cardholder's participation, while for other codes the evidence is different. Submit the evidence before the representment deadline, and do not argue the code itself if the evidence does not fit it.
questions.question: A merchant receives a chargeback with a fraud reason code and wants to dispute it, but their only evidence is that the customer is a regular buyer. You are the BA advising them. What evidence actually matters for this reason code, and what is the risk of disputing without it?

questions.answer: Treat it as a duplicate-processing case: confirm both charges have the same amount, merchant and authorisation reference, then refund one immediately and investigate why the merchant presented the transaction twice. Check whether a timeout caused a retry that created a second clearing record. Tell the customer one charge will be reversed and give them a date, rather than asking them to wait for the merchant.
questions.question: A customer was charged twice for one purchase and the merchant says only one payment was received. You are the BA investigating. How do you prove it is a duplicate, and who refunds the customer?

questions.answer: Tell the customer not to send the money again, because a UPI debit with no credit is usually a timeout where the payment may still settle or be reversed automatically. Check the transaction status with the reference, and if it is still pending, wait for the system to resolve it within the defined window before raising a complaint. If it remains unresolved after that window, raise a dispute and give the customer a reference number.
questions.question: A customer pays by UPI, the money is debited, but the recipient says nothing arrived, and the app shows the payment timed out. The customer wants to pay again immediately. You are the BA on the support call. What do you tell them, and why?

questions.answer: Explain that UPI payments are effectively irrevocable once executed, so the bank cannot pull the money back from the recipient's account without their consent. Start a recall or request the recipient to return the funds, and ask the customer to verify the UPI ID before sending in future. Never promise a refund, because recovery depends on the recipient.
questions.question: A customer sends money to the wrong UPI ID and asks the bank to reverse it instantly. You are the BA explaining what is possible. Why is this different from cancelling a pending bank transfer, and what do you do next?

questions.answer: Check the Faster Payments limit, the beneficiary bank's availability and the payment status, because a payment can be sent but held if the receiving bank is offline or the amount exceeds a limit. If the payment was accepted, it should arrive within the scheme's timeframe, usually seconds to a couple of hours, and the customer should be given the reference to trace it. If it was rejected, explain the reason and offer an alternative rail.
questions.question: A customer sends a Faster Payment on Friday night and the recipient has not received it by Saturday morning. They assume the payment is lost. You are the BA tracing it. What do you check, and what do you tell them?

questions.answer: Recommend FedNow for the urgent, time-critical payment because it settles in seconds, 24 hours a day, while ACH is a batch system that can take a working day or more. Use ACH for routine, low-cost bulk payments where same-day arrival is not needed. Show the stakeholder the cost difference against the cost of missing the deadline, so the choice is a business trade-off, not just a fee comparison.
questions.question: A US business needs to pay a supplier urgently and asks whether to use FedNow or ACH. You are the BA advising them. How do you choose, and what trade-off do you explain?

questions.answer: Do not assume the payment failed just because the beneficiary bank is offline; the payment may be queued and settle when the bank returns, or it may be rejected with a clear reason. Check the payment status, hold any duplicate instruction, and give the customer a realistic update time. If the payment is rejected, resend it only after confirming the original did not settle.
questions.question: An instant payment is sent to a beneficiary bank that is offline for maintenance, and the sender wants to know whether the money is lost. You are the BA handling the case. What do you check, and what do you tell the sender?

questions.answer: Explain the difference clearly: a reversal cancels the original transaction before settlement, while a refund after settlement is a new payment back to the customer and takes the normal clearing time. If the transaction has already settled, offer a refund with a realistic timescale and a reference, rather than promising an instant reversal. Log the merchant's request so the refund can be traced if the customer queries it.
questions.question: A merchant wants to reverse a card payment the day after the sale, but the transaction has already settled. They insist a reversal should be instant. You are the BA explaining the options. What is the difference between a reversal and a refund here?

questions.answer: Explain that interchange is the fee the acquirer pays the issuer, set by the scheme, and it is only one part of the merchant's total cost, which also includes scheme fees and the acquirer's margin. A premium card, a cross-border transaction or a card-not-present sale carries a higher interchange rate because the risk and cost are higher. Show the merchant the breakdown by transaction type so they can see which sales are driving the cost, rather than quoting a single average rate.
questions.question: A merchant complains their card fees have risen and blames the bank, but most of their sales are now premium cards online. You are the BA explaining interchange. How do you show them why the fees changed?

questions.answer: Check whether the mandate is linked to the old card or a token, and whether the token was updated when the card expired. If the mandate is tied to an expired card number, the payment will keep failing until the customer updates their card details. Proactively notify customers before expiry, offer an in-app update flow, and pause retries after the first failure so you do not keep attempting a dead card.
questions.question: A recurring card payment fails every month after the customer's card expires, and support keeps retrying it. You are the BA fixing the process. Why does it keep failing, and what should happen instead?

questions.answer: Explain that the merchant's sales are cleared and settled in batches, and a weekend sale may not settle until the next working day, even though the customer was authorised immediately. Show the merchant the clearing cut-off and the settlement calendar, and offer faster settlement only if the acquirer supports it and the cost is agreed. Do not promise same-day settlement for a weekend sale unless the contract says so.
questions.question: A merchant makes sales all weekend but the money does not reach their account until Tuesday, and they accuse the acquirer of holding their funds. You are the BA explaining card clearing and settlement. What do you tell them?

questions.answer: Advise the merchant that surcharging is restricted or banned in many markets and by some schemes, and that a surcharge can drive customers away and breach their acquirer agreement. Suggest instead that they review their pricing, negotiate their acquirer fees, or offer a cheaper payment method as an option. Check the local rules and the scheme rules before giving a final answer, as they vary by country.
questions.question: A merchant wants to add a surcharge to every card payment to cover their fees. You are the BA advising them. Why might this be a bad idea, and what do you check before saying yes or no?

questions.answer: Act immediately: block the token on the lost device, check for any transactions after the loss, and issue a new token for the replacement device. The underlying card number does not need to change if only the device token is compromised, which is one of the benefits of tokenisation. Tell the customer which transactions were blocked and confirm the new token is active before they try to pay again.
questions.question: A customer loses their phone with a tokenised card in their wallet, and a payment is attempted from the device. You are the BA on the incident. What do you do first, and why does tokenisation help here?

questions.answer: Explain that liability shifts to the issuer when 3DS authentication succeeds, so the merchant is generally protected against a fraud chargeback for that transaction. If the merchant skipped 3DS or used an exemption, the liability usually stays with the merchant. Use this to justify the extra friction for high-risk transactions, and log the authentication result with the transaction so it can be used as evidence later.
questions.question: A merchant skips 3DS to speed up checkout, then receives a fraud chargeback and expects the issuer to bear the loss. You are the BA explaining liability shift. Who bears the loss here, and why?

questions.answer: Do not let the deadline pass silently, because a missed representment deadline usually means the chargeback stands and the merchant loses the funds. Escalate the case immediately, check whether the scheme allows a late submission or a pre-arbitration, and record the miss as a process failure. Fix the workflow so cases are flagged days before the deadline, not on the day it expires.
questions.question: A merchant misses the deadline to dispute a chargeback and the money is taken from their account. They ask you to reopen the case. You are the BA handling it. What options remain, and what process fix do you propose?

questions.answer: Block the card, refund the fraudulent contactless transactions after investigation, and check whether the contactless limit or the cumulative limit allowed the fraud to continue. Explain to the customer that contactless is designed for low-value convenience, which is why limits exist, and that a PIN would have been required for larger amounts. Offer a replacement card and review whether the fraud pattern suggests a stolen card rather than a lost one.
questions.question: A customer's lost card is used for several small contactless payments before they report it. They ask why the bank did not stop the payments. You are the BA investigating. What do you check, and how do you explain the contactless limits?

questions.answer: Check the autopay mandate status, the UPI daily limit and the account balance, because a mandate can fail if the limit is reached, the mandate expired, or the account has insufficient funds. Notify the customer before the payment date so they can fix the issue, and retry once on a defined schedule rather than repeatedly. If the mandate has expired, ask the customer to set up a new one.
questions.question: A customer's UPI autopay for a subscription fails every month, but a manual UPI payment works. You are the BA diagnosing the difference. What do you check, and what do you tell the customer?

questions.answer: Treat the second payment as a duplicate and block it, because a retry after a timeout can create two payments if the first one actually succeeded. Check the transaction references and the account to confirm whether the first payment settled, and only resend if you can prove it did not. Build idempotency into the retry logic so the same instruction ID cannot create two payments.
questions.question: A real-time payment times out and the system automatically retries it, so the beneficiary is paid twice. You are the BA reviewing the incident. What went wrong in the retry design, and what do you change?

questions.answer: Explain that the hold is an authorisation to guarantee funds, not a charge, and it will be released when the final amount is presented or after the hold period expires. Show the customer the hold amount, the final charge and the expected release date, and ask the merchant to release the hold early if the final amount is already known. Do not promise an instant release unless the merchant has confirmed it.
questions.question: A customer hires a car, sees a large authorisation hold on their card, and insists they have been charged for the hire before they even drive it. You are the BA explaining the hold. What do you tell them, and what can the merchant do?

questions.answer: Advise the customer to choose the local currency if their card offers a good exchange rate, because dynamic currency conversion usually adds a margin and the merchant's rate is rarely better. Explain that the choice is made at the point of sale and cannot be changed after authorisation. If the customer was not given a clear choice, log it as a merchant practice issue and explain the difference for next time.
questions.question: A customer pays by card abroad, is offered to pay in their home currency, and later realises the amount was higher than expected. You are the BA explaining dynamic currency conversion. What should they have chosen, and why?

questions.answer: Explain that instant payments are irrevocable once executed, so the bank cannot pull the money back without the recipient's consent. Start a recall request, contact the receiving bank, and ask the customer to check the account details with the recipient. Never promise a refund, and use the case to argue for a confirmation-of-payee check before the payment is sent.
questions.question: A customer sends an instant payment to the wrong account and expects the bank to reverse it immediately because it was instant. You are the BA on the call. Why is instant actually harder to reverse, and what do you do?

questions.answer: Tell the merchant plainly that storing full card numbers breaches PCI-DSS and creates a serious data-breach risk, and that the fine and reputational cost far outweigh the convenience. Offer tokenisation or a compliant payment service provider that stores the card securely on their behalf. If they refuse, escalate to risk and compliance, because this is not a business preference but a security requirement.
questions.question: A merchant wants to store customers' full card numbers in a spreadsheet to speed up repeat orders. You are the BA who has to stop them. What do you say, and what compliant alternative do you offer?

questions.answer: Check the reason code first, because a goods-not-received claim needs delivery evidence, not just a statement that the customer paid. Ask the merchant for tracking, proof of delivery and any customer communication, and submit it before the deadline. If there is no delivery evidence, advise the merchant to refund rather than dispute, as a weak dispute can lead to further scheme fees.
questions.question: A merchant receives a chargeback saying goods were not received, but they say they posted the order. You are the BA advising them. What evidence do you ask for, and when would you advise them not to dispute it?

questions.answer: Explain that a refund is a new payment that must clear and settle, so it takes the normal card timeline, often a few working days, even though the merchant initiated it immediately. Give the customer the refund reference, the amount and the expected date, and check the refund status if it has not arrived by then. Do not promise same-day credit unless the issuer supports instant refunds.
questions.question: A customer returns an item, the merchant refunds them on the spot, but the money does not appear for three days. The customer accuses the merchant of lying. You are the BA explaining refund timing. What do you tell them?

questions.answer: Explain that a card-present transaction is lower risk because the card and often a PIN are verified at the till, while a card-not-present transaction relies on the card details alone and is easier to use fraudulently. That is why online transactions attract higher interchange, more fraud checks and 3DS. Use this to justify the extra authentication for online sales, rather than treating both channels as the same risk.
questions.question: A stakeholder asks why online card payments face more fraud checks and higher fees than in-store payments. You are the BA explaining card-present versus card-not-present risk. What is the difference, and what follows from it?

questions.answer: Plan a token migration, not a card-number migration: work with the payment provider to move tokens from the old provider to the new one, or ask customers to re-enter their card once if token portability is not available. Test the migration on a small group, check that recurring payments continue, and communicate the change to customers in advance. Never copy full card numbers between providers to avoid the migration work.
questions.question: Your company is switching payment providers and has thousands of stored subscriptions. You are the BA planning the migration. How do you move the recurring payments without asking every customer to re-enter their card?

questions.answer: Do not split the payment to fit the limit, because splitting can look like an attempt to bypass a control and it creates two reconciliation items for one invoice. Check whether a higher limit, a different rail or a high-value payment system is available for this amount. If none is available, agree a staged payment plan with the supplier and document why it was split.
questions.question: A business needs to pay an amount above the Faster Payments limit and suggests splitting it into two smaller payments. You are the BA advising them. Why is splitting risky, and what do you offer instead?

questions.answer: Recommend FedNow for urgent, time-critical payments and ACH for routine bulk payments, based on speed, cost and the recipient's ability to receive instant payments. Check the amount limits and the operating hours for each rail before promising a time. Present the choice as a trade-off between speed and cost, with the business impact of a delay made explicit.
questions.question: A US finance team asks you to set a default rail for all supplier payments, choosing between FedNow and ACH. You are the BA setting the policy. Why is a single default the wrong answer, and what rule do you propose?

questions.answer: Treat the collect request as suspicious until proven otherwise, because fraudsters use collect requests to trick people into approving a payment to them. Check the requester's identity, the amount and whether the customer was expecting it, and advise the customer never to approve a collect request they did not expect. Report the request to the fraud team and block the requester if it is confirmed as fraud.
questions.question: A customer receives a UPI collect request from an unknown person asking them to approve a payment, and they are unsure whether to accept it. You are the BA advising them. What do you tell them, and what action do you take?

questions.answer: Distinguish friendly fraud, where a genuine customer disputes a legitimate purchase, from true fraud, where the card was used without permission. Check the delivery address, device, authentication and purchase history, and if the evidence shows the customer received the goods, dispute the chargeback with that evidence. If the pattern repeats, flag the customer for review rather than treating each dispute in isolation.
questions.question: A customer repeatedly buys goods, receives them, then claims the card was used fraudulently. You are the BA investigating the pattern. How do you tell friendly fraud from true fraud, and what do you do?

questions.answer: Explain that interchange-plus pricing shows the scheme and interchange costs separately from the acquirer's margin, so the merchant can see exactly what is driving the total. A flat rate hides this but is simpler to budget for. Recommend interchange-plus for a merchant with varied transaction types who wants transparency, and a flat rate only if they value predictability over detail.
questions.question: A merchant is offered interchange-plus pricing and a flat-rate deal, and asks which is better. You are the BA comparing them. How do you explain the trade-off, and which would you recommend for a merchant with mixed sales?

questions.answer: Plan for 24-hour operations from the start: real-time payments have no batch window to fix problems overnight, so you need monitoring, alerting and an on-call rota. Design the incident playbook for a 2am failure, including how to pause the service, communicate to customers and reconcile the payments that were in flight. Do not launch a 24x7 service with a 9-to-5 support model.
questions.question: Your bank is launching a 24x7 instant payment service, but support only works 9 to 5. You are the BA flagging the risk. What breaks at 2am when a payment fails, and what operating model do you propose?

questions.answer: Check whether the settlement is delayed by a weekend, a scheme cut-off or an acquirer failure, and confirm the merchant's expected settlement date in the contract. If the acquirer has failed to settle on time, escalate to the acquirer and the scheme, and give the merchant a clear revised date. Do not tell the merchant the money is lost until you have confirmed the settlement status with the acquirer.
questions.question: A merchant's card settlement does not arrive on the expected day and they cannot pay their suppliers. You are the BA tracing the settlement. What do you check, and what do you tell the merchant?

questions.answer: Use exemptions only where the risk is genuinely low, for example a low-value transaction from a known customer on a trusted device, and keep the exemption logic transparent so risk can audit it. Do not exempt high-value or first-time transactions, as that defeats the purpose of strong customer authentication. Review the exemption rate regularly and tighten it if fraud rises.
questions.question: Product wants to exempt as many transactions as possible from 3DS to improve conversion. You are the BA setting the exemption policy. Where do you allow exemptions, and where do you refuse?

questions.answer: Explain that pre-arbitration is the stage after a chargeback dispute where the issuer disagrees with the merchant's representment, and the scheme will decide if it goes to arbitration. Check whether the new evidence is strong enough to justify the arbitration fee, which the loser usually pays. If the evidence is weak, advise the merchant to accept the chargeback rather than risk the extra fee.
questions.question: A merchant's chargeback dispute is rejected and the case moves to pre-arbitration, with a fee if they lose. They want to fight it on principle. You are the BA advising them. What do you tell them about the cost and the odds?

questions.answer: Explain that cancelling with the merchant stops the service, but the bank mandate may still be active and the merchant could present another collection. Tell the customer to cancel both: with the merchant to end the service, and with the bank to stop the mandate. Confirm the mandate is closed and check the next collection date to make sure no further payment goes out.
questions.question: A customer cancels a subscription with the merchant, but a further payment is still taken. They say they cancelled, so the bank should have stopped it. You are the BA explaining the gap. What went wrong, and what should the customer have done?

questions.answer: Mark the payment as status unknown, reconcile it against the account and the rail before deciding, and do not resend it until you have proved it did not settle. Give the customer a reference and a timescale for the investigation, and prioritise the case if the amount is high or the customer is waiting for goods. Build a dashboard that shows unknown-status payments separately, so they are not hidden in the success count.
questions.question: An instant payment shows as status unknown after a system outage, and the customer is waiting for goods that depend on it. You are the BA handling the case. What do you do first, and how do you keep the customer informed?

questions.answer: Explain that an offline authorisation is approved by the card chip without contacting the issuer, usually for low-value transactions when the terminal is offline. The risk is that the issuer cannot check the balance or fraud status in real time, so offline limits are kept low. If the transaction later declines when it is presented, the merchant bears the risk, which is why offline authorisation is limited.
questions.question: A shop's terminal is offline and still approves a card payment, but the payment later fails. The merchant asks how a payment can be approved and then fail. You are the BA explaining offline authorisation. What do you tell them?

questions.answer: Check the UPI daily limit, the per-transaction limit and the bank's own limit, because a business payment can hit any of these even if the account has funds. Offer to split the payment across days only if the supplier agrees, or use a different rail for the larger amount. Do not ask the customer to use a personal account to bypass the business limit, as that creates a control and audit problem.
questions.question: A small business hits its UPI daily limit halfway through paying suppliers and asks you to raise it on the spot. You are the BA handling the request. What do you check, and what alternatives do you offer?

questions.answer: Check the reason code, because a services-not-rendered claim needs proof that the service was provided or was available, such as a booking, a contract or evidence the customer used the service. If the merchant can prove the service was delivered, dispute it with that evidence; if they cannot, advise a refund. Do not dispute on the basis that the customer is being unreasonable, as the scheme decides on evidence, not on fairness.
questions.question: A customer books a service, does not turn up, and then raises a chargeback saying the service was not rendered. The merchant wants to dispute it. You are the BA advising them. What evidence matters, and when should they not dispute?

questions.answer: Do not launch instant refunds without a fraud check, because instant refunds are a prime target for fraudsters who buy, refund and keep the goods. Propose a risk-based approach: instant refunds for low-risk, verified returns, and standard refunds for higher-risk cases. Show product the fraud loss from a no-check launch against the conversion gain, so the decision is made on numbers, not on speed alone.
questions.question: Product wants to launch instant card refunds for all customers to beat a competitor, with no fraud check. You are the BA on the project. What risk do you flag, and what compromise do you propose?

questions.answer: Push back on Excel-only, because a daily reconciliation needs a controlled, repeatable process with a clear data source, matching rules and an audit trail. Propose a three-way match between the gateway, the bank statement and the ledger, with automatic matching for exact items and a manual queue for breaks. Show the stakeholder the cost of a missed break, such as a duplicate payment or a lost receipt, against the cost of a proper tool.
questions.question: You are the BA asked to build a daily reconciliation process from scratch, and a stakeholder says a spreadsheet checked once a week is enough. What process do you propose instead, and how do you justify it?

questions.answer: First check whether the difference is a fee, a foreign exchange difference or a timing difference, by comparing the gateway amount, the bank amount and the ledger amount line by line. If it is a fee deducted by the bank or an intermediary, record it as a fee and match the net amount, rather than leaving it as a break. If it is a genuine mismatch, raise it as an exception with the exact difference and the source documents.
questions.question: Your daily reconciliation shows the gateway amount is higher than the bank amount for the same payment. You are the BA investigating the break. What are the most likely causes, and how do you resolve each one?

questions.answer: Do not force the nostro to balance by posting a plug figure, because that hides the real cause and creates a bigger problem later. Break the difference down by value date, currency and transaction type, and check for missing statements, duplicate entries, fees and cut-off items. Escalate to treasury with the aged breakdown, and agree a funding or correction plan for each item.
questions.question: Your nostro account does not balance at month end and treasury wants you to post a balancing entry so the books can close. You are the BA who has to refuse. Why is a plug figure dangerous, and what do you do instead?

questions.answer: Confirm it is a true duplicate by matching the instruction ID, amount, beneficiary, value date and reference, not just the amount. If both payments were executed, recall one and refund the beneficiary, and log the duplicate as a control failure. Fix the root cause, usually a retry after a timeout without an idempotency check, so the same instruction cannot be executed twice.
questions.question: Reconciliation shows two identical payments to the same supplier on the same day. The supplier says they received both. You are the BA handling the duplicate. How do you confirm it is a duplicate, and what do you do with the extra payment?

questions.answer: Check whether the payment is a timing difference, for example it was executed after the bank cut-off or the statement was cut before it arrived, before treating it as missing. Compare the ledger date, the value date and the bank statement date, and look for the payment in the next day's statement. If it is still missing after the next cycle, raise a trace with the bank and the rail, and do not write it off.
questions.question: A payment appears in the ledger but not on the bank statement. Your manager assumes it is lost. You are the BA investigating. What do you check first, and when do you treat it as genuinely missing?

questions.answer: Spot the pattern by comparing the digits: a transposition swaps two adjacent digits, so the difference is often divisible by nine and the amounts look similar. Confirm the correct amount from the source instruction and the invoice, then correct the ledger entry with a clear audit trail. Add a validation check that flags amounts close to but not equal to the expected amount, so the next transposition is caught at entry.
questions.question: A reconciliation break is for a small amount and the digits look swapped, for example 1,234 against 1,324. You are the BA investigating. How do you prove it is a transposition error, and what control do you add?

questions.answer: Check the exchange rate used by each system and the date it was applied, because a rate difference between initiation and settlement creates a genuine foreign exchange break. Agree a single rate source and a tolerance for small differences, and book the difference as a foreign exchange gain or loss with approval. If the difference is larger than the tolerance, investigate whether the wrong rate or the wrong currency was used.
questions.question: A cross-border payment reconciles in the foreign currency but not in your base currency, and the difference is a foreign exchange amount. You are the BA resolving the break. How do you decide whether it is a genuine FX difference or an error?

questions.answer: Check the value dates on both sides, because a payment can be recorded in the ledger on Friday but value-dated Monday by the bank, creating a timing break that will clear on Monday. Do not treat it as a missing payment until the value date has passed. Record it as a timing difference with the expected clearance date, and review it again on that date.
questions.question: A payment shows as a break on Friday but you suspect it is only a value-date difference. You are the BA deciding whether to raise it as an exception. How do you confirm it, and what do you record?

questions.answer: Escalate the aged items to the owners with a deadline, because a suspense balance that is 90 days old means the underlying payment has not been investigated or resolved. For each item, decide whether it can be allocated, refunded or written off, and get approval for any write-off. Report the aging to the auditor with the action plan, rather than letting the balance grow silently.
questions.question: Your suspense account has items over 90 days old and an auditor asks why they are still there. You are the BA owning the account. What do you do about the aged items, and what do you tell the auditor?

questions.answer: Start with the pacs.002 reason code, because it tells you whether the fault is in the account number, the amount, a duplicate or a regulatory issue. For an incorrect account number, correct the details and send a new payment; for a duplicate, block any resend; for a regulatory reject, escalate to compliance. Never resend the same payment without reading the code, as that can create a duplicate or a second reject.
questions.question: A payment fails and you receive a pacs.002 reject message, but operations wants to resend the payment immediately. You are the BA who has to stop them. Why must you read the reject code first, and what do you do with it?

questions.answer: Treat each return code differently: R01 usually means insufficient funds, so check the account and retry only if funds are now available; R03 usually means no account or unable to locate the account, so correct the account details before any retry; AC03 usually means an invalid creditor account number, so do not retry until the beneficiary confirms the correct number. Log the code, the action and the customer communication for each case, so the same return is not retried blindly.
questions.question: You receive three returns in one morning with codes R01, R03 and AC03, and operations wants to retry all three. You are the BA triaging them. What does each code mean for your next step, and which would you not retry?

questions.answer: Do not leave the cash unapplied indefinitely, because it will age in suspense and the customer may be chased for a debt they have already paid. Search by amount, date and payer name, contact the customer for the invoice reference, and allocate the payment once you have evidence. If you cannot identify the payer after a defined period, follow the unapplied-cash policy for a refund or a write-off with approval.
questions.question: A customer pays an invoice but gives no reference, so the cash sits unapplied and the customer is chased for payment. You are the BA fixing the process. How do you allocate the cash, and what do you change to stop it happening again?

questions.answer: Do not close with known breaks hidden, because that misstates the position and pushes the problem into the next month. Close with the breaks clearly listed, aged and owned, with a plan and a date for each, and get the CFO to sign off on the open items. Report the impact of each break, such as a missing receipt or a duplicate payment, so the close is honest about what is unresolved.
questions.question: It is month end, several reconciliation breaks are still unresolved, and the CFO wants the books closed today. You are the BA who has to close honestly. What do you do, and what do you refuse to do?

questions.answer: Work in order: confirm the payment status in your system, check the rail and the bank, then check the beneficiary bank and any intermediary hold. At each step, record what you found and the reference, so the next person does not repeat the work. Give the customer a single update with the current stage and the next check, rather than a series of vague promises.
questions.question: A high-value payment is stuck and the customer is escalating hourly. You are the BA running the investigation. What is your step-by-step workflow, and how do you keep the customer informed without guessing?

questions.answer: Propose SLAs by risk and value, not a single deadline for all exceptions: high-value and customer-impacting breaks get same-day action, while low-value timing differences get a longer window. Report exceptions by age, value and owner, with a clear escalation path when an SLA is breached. Do not hide aged items by re-dating them, as that breaks the audit trail and the SLA itself.
questions.question: Operations wants one SLA for all reconciliation exceptions, and a manager suggests re-dating aged items so the SLA looks green. You are the BA setting the SLA and reporting. What do you propose, and why do you refuse to re-date items?

questions.answer: Check the intermediary's fee schedule and the payment instruction, because some intermediaries deduct their fee from the amount sent, so the beneficiary receives less than the instructed amount. Record the fee separately and match the net amount, and tell the sender in advance that the beneficiary may receive less. If the deduction was not agreed, raise it with the intermediary and consider a different route next time.
questions.question: A beneficiary receives less than the amount sent because an intermediary bank deducted a fee, and reconciliation shows a break. You are the BA resolving it. Is this an error, and how do you match it?

questions.answer: Check the file's control totals and the instruction IDs, because a duplicate in a bulk file is usually a repeated line or a file sent twice. Block the duplicate items before execution if they have not yet been sent, and recall any that have already been executed. Tell the employer exactly which items were duplicated and confirm the file will not be reprocessed in full.
questions.question: A bulk payroll file is uploaded twice by mistake and some employees are paid twice. You are the BA on the incident. How do you stop the second run, and what do you do about the employees already paid twice?

questions.answer: Check the cut-off times on both sides, because a nostro payment sent after the cut-off will be value-dated the next working day and will appear as a break until then. Record it as a timing difference with the expected value date, and do not treat it as missing. Fix the process so payments are submitted before the cut-off, or the customer is told the next value date up front.
questions.question: A nostro break appears every Friday and clears on Monday, and the team treats it as a recurring error. You are the BA investigating the pattern. What is the likely cause, and how do you stop the weekly false alarm?

questions.answer: Design the controls into the process from the start: segregation of duties so the person who creates a payment cannot approve it, a maker-checker for high-value items, and a daily reconciliation with an independent review. Log every manual adjustment with a reason and an approver, so no one can change a break without a trail. Show the stakeholder that these controls prevent a single person from hiding an error or a fraud.
questions.question: You are the BA designing a new reconciliation process and a stakeholder says controls will slow the team down. What controls do you insist on, and how do you justify them?

questions.answer: Do not write off a suspense item without evidence and approval, because it may belong to a customer who is still waiting for their money. Investigate the item, try to allocate or refund it, and only write it off with a documented reason and a senior approval. Report all write-offs to the auditor with the investigation notes, so the decision can be reviewed.
questions.question: A suspense item cannot be allocated after weeks of investigation and a manager asks you to write it off to clear the account. You are the BA deciding whether to agree. What do you require before a write-off, and why?

questions.answer: Reopen the prior period only if the policy allows it, and record the return as a prior-period adjustment with a clear audit trail, rather than silently changing the closed figures. Check whether the return affects the customer's account, the ledger and the bank, and reconcile all three. Tell the finance team the impact on the closed period so they can decide whether to restate or to book it in the current period.
questions.question: A payment is returned after the month has already closed and reconciled. You are the BA handling the late return. How do you record it without corrupting the closed period?

questions.answer: Treat it as a timing difference if the amounts match and the dates differ by the expected settlement lag, and record it with the expected clearance date. If the lag is longer than normal, investigate whether the bank or the rail is delayed. Do not force a match by changing a date, as that hides a genuine delay.
questions.question: The ledger and the bank show the same payment on different dates, and the team wants to force them to match by changing the ledger date. You are the BA reviewing the break. When is this a timing difference, and why do you refuse to change the date?

questions.answer: Agree a single rate source and a single rate date for the reconciliation, and record the source with each item so a rate dispute can be settled from the evidence.
