If the counterparty used a different rate, show them the agreed source and the tolerance, and book the difference as a foreign exchange item. Do not use a rate chosen after the event to make the numbers match.
questions.question: Your team and a counterparty disagree on the exchange rate for a payment, and each side's reconciliation shows a different break. You are the BA resolving the dispute. How do you decide which rate is correct?

questions.answer: Treat the gateway timeout as a status-unknown case, not as a failure: check the gateway, the bank and the ledger before deciding whether the payment executed. If it did execute, match it and tell the customer it succeeded; if it did not, resend it once with a new instruction ID. Log the timeout as a system incident so the retry logic can be reviewed.
questions.question: A payment times out at the gateway and reconciliation shows it as pending, but the customer says the money left their account. You are the BA investigating. How do you decide whether the payment succeeded?

questions.answer: Prioritise by a combination of value, age and customer impact, not by value alone: a high-value break gets immediate attention, an old low-value break gets attention because it is aging, and a customer-impacting break gets priority even if the value is low. Use a scoring rule so the queue is transparent and no one can cherry-pick easy items. Report the queue by these bands so management can see the real risk.
questions.question: Your exception queue has 200 items and the team is working on the easiest ones first. You are the BA setting the prioritisation. How do you decide what gets worked first, and how do you stop cherry-picking?

questions.answer: Push back on 100 percent auto-matching, because some items will always need judgement, such as fees, foreign exchange differences and timing differences. Propose auto-matching for exact matches and a tolerance for small differences, with the rest going to a manual queue. Show the stakeholder the false matches that a loose rule would create, and agree a realistic auto-match rate with a review of the manual queue.
questions.question: A stakeholder insists the new reconciliation system should auto-match 100 percent of items with no manual work. You are the BA setting the matching rules. Why is that unrealistic, and what target do you propose instead?

questions.answer: Design reconciliation to run continuously, not just at end of day, because instant payments settle 24 hours a day and a break at 2am is already a customer problem by morning. Use intraday matching, alerting for high-value breaks, and a rota that covers the overnight period. Do not wait for the next morning's batch to discover a failure that happened overnight.
questions.question: Your bank launches 24x7 instant payments but reconciliation still runs once a day at midnight. You are the BA flagging the gap. What breaks, and what reconciliation model do you propose?

questions.answer: Search by amount, date and payer, contact the customer for the reference, and allocate the payment once you have evidence, rather than guessing from a similar invoice. If the customer cannot be identified, hold the cash in suspense with a clear owner and a review date. Never allocate unapplied cash to the oldest invoice by default, as that can misstate the customer's account and hide a dispute.
questions.question: A large payment arrives with no reference and no payer name that matches any customer. You are the BA deciding what to do with it. How do you try to allocate it, and what must you not do?

questions.answer: Read the code first: AC04 usually means the creditor account is closed, so do not retry the payment to the same account. Contact the beneficiary for new account details, verify them, and send a new payment once they are confirmed. Tell the sender the account is closed and give them the new expected date, rather than leaving the payment in a failed state with no action.
questions.question: A payment is rejected with pacs.002 code AC04 and operations wants to retry it tomorrow. You are the BA triaging the reject. What does the code mean, and why would a retry fail again?

questions.answer: Treat AM05 as a duplicate-payment reject, which means the payment was already received, so do not resend it. Check the original payment's status and confirm it settled, then tell the sender the payment was already made. Fix the retry logic so the same instruction ID cannot be sent twice after a timeout.
questions.question: A payment is rejected with pacs.002 code AM05 after a timeout and a retry. You are the BA investigating. What does the code tell you, and what is the risk if operations retries it again?

questions.answer: Check the mandate record first, because a missing or invalid mandate means the collection was not authorised and the bank may have to refund it. If the mandate was cancelled or never existed, process the refund and stop future collections. If the mandate exists but was not linked correctly, fix the linkage and show the customer the mandate evidence.
questions.question: A direct debit collection is rejected because the mandate is missing, and the customer says they never agreed to it. You are the BA investigating. What do you check first, and when do you refund?

questions.answer: Explain that the money was returned to the sender's account and, if the sender has already spent it, the return creates a shortfall that must be recovered. Contact the sender immediately, agree a repayment plan, and do not simply re-debit the account without notice. Record the return, the shortfall and the recovery plan so the case is not lost in reconciliation.
questions.question: A payment is returned after the recipient has already spent the money, and the sender's account is now overdrawn. You are the BA handling the case. What do you tell the sender, and how do you recover the funds?

questions.answer: Do not accept a refusal as the end of the case: send a formal recall request with the evidence that the payment was a duplicate, and ask the beneficiary bank to contact their customer. If the beneficiary still refuses, log the loss, escalate to the legal or recovery team, and review the control that allowed the duplicate. Tell the sender honestly what recovery options remain and what the likely outcome is.
questions.question: A duplicate payment was sent and the beneficiary refuses to return the extra money, saying it was a payment they were owed. You are the BA handling the recovery. What do you do next, and what do you tell the sender?

questions.answer: Break the nostro difference down by currency, value date and transaction type, and check for a foreign exchange rate difference, a fee, or a payment that was recorded in the wrong currency. Confirm the rate source and the date used on each side, and correct the entry that used the wrong rate. Do not book the difference as a fee or a loss until you have proved the cause.
questions.question: Your nostro account shows a break in a foreign currency, and the team assumes it is a fee. You are the BA investigating. How do you prove whether it is an FX difference, a fee, or a wrong-currency entry?

questions.answer: Trace the payment from the ledger to the suspense account with the reference, amount and date, and show the customer where it is and why it was held. Explain that suspense is a holding account for items that cannot yet be allocated, not a lost account, and give them a date for the allocation or refund. If the item has been in suspense too long, escalate it and agree the next step with the customer.
questions.question: A customer says their money is lost because it is sitting in a suspense account. You are the BA explaining the position. What do you tell them, and what action do you take to resolve it?

questions.answer: Reconcile intercompany items separately, because they involve two entities in the same group and a break in one is a break in the other. Agree the amounts, dates and references with the other entity before month end, and do not close until both sides agree. If they do not agree, record the difference as an open item with an owner and a date, rather than forcing a match.
questions.question: An intercompany payment is recorded differently by two entities in the same group, and both sides want to close month end. You are the BA reconciling it. How do you get both sides to agree, and what if they cannot?

questions.answer: Report the exception position honestly: total open breaks by value, age and owner, the oldest items, the SLA compliance rate, and the trend over the last three months. Highlight the high-risk items, such as high-value or customer-impacting breaks, separately from low-value timing differences. Do not present a single total that hides the aging, as the board needs to see the risk, not just the count.
questions.question: You are the BA preparing an exception report for senior management. A manager wants to show only the total number of open breaks. What else must the report show, and why is a single total misleading?

questions.answer: Start with data quality: agree the source systems, the fields to match on, the tolerances and the cut-off times before building any matching logic. Test the rules on historical data to see the auto-match rate and the false-match rate, and fix the source data where it is incomplete. A reconciliation built on bad data will produce breaks that are really data errors, not payment errors.
questions.question: You are the BA building a reconciliation from scratch and the source data is incomplete, with missing references and inconsistent amounts. A stakeholder wants the matching logic built first. Why do you insist on fixing the data first?

questions.answer: Allocate the partial payment to the invoice the customer intended, or to the oldest invoice only if the customer confirms that is what they meant. Contact the customer to confirm the allocation and the remaining balance, and do not treat the invoice as fully paid. Record the partial payment clearly so the customer is not chased for the full amount.
questions.question: A customer pays part of an invoice with no reference, and the system allocates it to the wrong invoice. You are the BA fixing the allocation. How do you decide where the partial payment belongs?

questions.answer: Check the bank statement for charges that were not recorded in the ledger, such as a monthly fee or a transaction charge, and book them with the correct date and account. Update the ledger process so bank charges are captured automatically, rather than being discovered at reconciliation. If the charge is unexpected, query it with the bank before booking it.
questions.question: Reconciliation shows a break equal to a bank charge that was never recorded in the ledger. You are the BA investigating. Is this a payment error, and how do you fix the process so it does not recur?

questions.answer: Reconcile card settlements in three steps: the merchant's sales, the acquirer's settlement file, and the bank credit. If the bank credit is less than the sales, check for fees, chargebacks and refunds deducted before settlement. Give the merchant a settlement breakdown by day, so they can see the deductions rather than a single net amount.
questions.question: A merchant's card settlement is less than their sales for the day and they accuse the acquirer of short-paying them. You are the BA reconciling the settlement. What deductions do you check, and what do you show the merchant?

questions.answer: Compare the gateway settlement file with the bank credit line by line, checking the settlement date, the batch total and any deductions for fees or refunds. If a batch is missing, check whether it was settled on the next working day or held by the gateway. Raise a query with the gateway with the batch reference and the expected amount, and do not write off the difference.
questions.question: A gateway settlement batch does not appear on the bank statement on the expected day. You are the BA tracing it. What do you check, and when do you raise it with the gateway?

questions.answer: Raise a trace with the intermediary using the payment reference, amount, value date and the last confirmed stage, and ask for the status and the reason for the hold. Give the customer a realistic update time and do not promise an arrival date you cannot verify. If the intermediary does not respond within the agreed time, escalate through the bank's correspondent relationship.
questions.question: A payment is stuck at an intermediary bank and the customer wants it traced. You are the BA running the trace. What information do you need, and what do you do if the intermediary does not respond?

questions.answer: Report the breach with the facts: which SLA was breached, how many items are affected, the value and age of the oldest item, and the impact on customers. Agree a recovery plan with owners and dates, and do not hide the breach by re-dating items or changing the SLA retrospectively. Use the breach to argue for more resource or a process fix, rather than treating it as a one-off.
questions.question: Your team breaches the exception SLA for the third month in a row and a manager suggests changing the SLA so it looks green. You are the BA reporting the breach. What do you report, and why do you refuse to change the SLA?

questions.answer: Check whether the same mandate was presented twice, for example because a file was sent twice or a retry created a second collection. Refund the duplicate collection immediately, stop any further presentation of that mandate, and fix the file control so the same mandate cannot be collected twice in one cycle. Tell the customer the refund date and confirm the mandate will only be collected once in future.
questions.question: A customer is charged twice by the same direct debit in one month. You are the BA investigating. How do you prove it is a duplicate collection, and what do you do about the extra debit?

questions.answer: Split the break into its components: first check the value-date difference, then the foreign exchange difference, and only then look for a genuine error. Use the agreed rate source and the value-date calendar to calculate each part separately. If the two parts explain the whole break, book them as timing and FX items; if a residual remains, investigate it as a separate break.
questions.question: A cross-border payment shows a break that could be a value-date difference, an FX difference, or both. You are the BA unpicking it. How do you separate the two causes?

questions.answer: Reconcile the opening balances first, because a migration error in the opening balance will create a break in every subsequent period. Compare the old system's closing balance with the new system's opening balance, item by item, and fix any differences before processing new items. Do not start daily reconciliation on a new system until the opening balance is agreed.
questions.question: After a system migration, reconciliation shows breaks from day one and the team blames the new system. You are the BA investigating. What do you check first, and why is the opening balance the most likely culprit?

questions.answer: Look for a pattern in the breaks, such as repeated small amounts to the same beneficiary, breaks that are always just below a threshold, or items that are repeatedly re-dated. Escalate the pattern to the fraud team with the evidence, and do not treat each break as an isolated error. Add a control that flags the pattern automatically, so it is caught before the next break.
questions.question: You notice a pattern in reconciliation breaks: small amounts to the same beneficiary, always just below the approval threshold. You are the BA who spots it. What do you do, and why must you not treat each break in isolation?

questions.answer: Check the reject code and the missing field, because BE04 usually relates to a missing or incomplete creditor address, which is required for some corridors. Ask the sender for the missing address, correct the instruction, and send a new payment. Do not resend the same instruction without the missing field, as it will be rejected again.
questions.question: A cross-border payment is rejected with pacs.002 code BE04 and the sender says the payment details were correct. You are the BA triaging the reject. What is the likely missing information, and what do you do?

questions.answer: Agree a cut-off for late items before month end, so items after the cut-off are booked in the next period and items before it are included in the current period. Communicate the cut-off to all teams, and do not move items between periods to make the numbers look better. Record any late item with its original date and the period it was booked in, so the audit trail is clear.
questions.question: Late payments arrive after the month-end cut-off and the finance team wants to include them in the closed month to improve the figures. You are the BA setting the cut-off. What rule do you set, and why do you refuse to move items between periods?

questions.answer: Contact the customer to confirm whether the overpayment was intentional, for example a payment on account, or a mistake. If it was a mistake, offer a refund or agree to hold it as a credit against the next invoice, and record the customer's choice. Do not allocate an overpayment to a future invoice without the customer's agreement, as that can hide a dispute.
questions.question: A customer overpays an invoice by a large amount and the system allocates the excess to their next invoice automatically. The customer asks for the money back. You are the BA handling the overpayment. What do you do, and what should the system not have done?

questions.answer: Check the nostro agent's fee schedule and the payment instruction, because some agents deduct their fee from the amount sent, creating a break between the instructed amount and the amount received. Record the fee separately, match the net amount, and tell the sender in advance that the agent's fee will be deducted. If the fee was not agreed, raise it with the agent and consider a different nostro agent.
questions.question: A nostro payment arrives short because the nostro agent deducted a fee, and the team treats it as a missing payment. You are the BA resolving the break. How do you prove it is a fee, and how do you match it?

questions.answer: Design the dashboard to show open breaks by age, value and owner, the SLA compliance rate, the oldest items, and the trend over time, with a drill-down to the individual break. Highlight high-value and customer-impacting items separately, so they are not hidden in the total. Make the dashboard available to the team and to management, so the same numbers are used by everyone.
questions.question: You are the BA designing an exception dashboard for the reconciliation team. A stakeholder wants a single green or red light. What does the dashboard actually need to show, and why is a single light not enough?

questions.answer: Investigate whether the failure is in the matching logic, the data or the process, by testing the rules on the failed items and checking the source data. If the rules are too strict, they will create false breaks; if they are too loose, they will create false matches. Fix the root cause and re-run the reconciliation, rather than manually clearing the breaks to make the numbers look good.
questions.question: Your new automated reconciliation system fails on its first day and the team wants to go back to spreadsheets. You are the BA diagnosing the failure. What do you check first, and when do you decide to fix it rather than abandon it?

questions.answer: Push back on weekly reconciliation for instant payments, because a payment that fails on Monday will not be discovered until the following week, by which time the customer has already escalated and the money may be lost. Propose daily reconciliation as a minimum, with intraday checks for high-value items. Show the stakeholder the cost of a week-old duplicate or missing payment against the cost of a daily check.
questions.question: A stakeholder wants to reconcile instant payments weekly to save effort, arguing that daily checks are overkill. You are the BA who has to refuse. What is the risk of a weekly cycle for a 24x7 payment service?

questions.answer: Do not release the payment, because a sanctions hit must be investigated before any funds move, and releasing it could breach the law and expose the bank to a fine. Hold the payment, check the screening result against the list, and escalate to compliance for a decision. Tell the customer only that the payment is under review and give them a timescale, without disclosing the screening detail.
questions.question: A high-value payment hits a sanctions screen and a stakeholder wants you to release it to keep an important customer happy. You are the BA on the case. Why do you refuse, and what do you do instead?

questions.answer: Treat it as a possible false positive first: compare the customer's full name, date of birth, address and other identifiers with the listed person, because a name alone is not enough to confirm a match. If the identifiers do not match, release the payment and record the false-positive decision with the evidence. If they do match, escalate to compliance and do not release the payment.
questions.question: A customer's payment is held because their name is similar to a name on a sanctions list, but the date of birth and address are different. You are the BA reviewing the hit. How do you decide whether it is a false positive, and what do you do?

questions.answer: Explain the difference clearly: freezing means the funds are held and cannot be used, blocking means the payment or transaction is stopped, and rejecting means the payment is returned to the sender. Freezing usually applies to an account or funds already held, while rejecting applies to a payment that has not yet been executed. Tell the customer what has happened to their specific payment, what they can and cannot do, and who to contact, without giving legal advice.
questions.question: A customer's account is frozen and they ask whether their money has been taken by the bank. You are the BA explaining freezing versus blocking versus rejecting. What is the difference, and what do you tell the customer?

questions.answer: Escalate the pattern to the AML team, because several payments just below a reporting threshold can be structuring, which is splitting a large amount to avoid detection. Do not warn the customer that they are under investigation, as that could be tipping off. Record the pattern, the amounts and the dates, and let the AML team decide whether to file a report.
questions.question: You notice a customer making several payments just below a reporting threshold, every day, to different accounts. You are the BA who spots the pattern. What do you do, and what must you not tell the customer?

questions.answer: Explain that the payment cannot proceed until KYC is complete, because the bank must verify the customer's identity and understand the purpose of the account before it can process payments. Ask the customer for the missing documents, give them a clear list and a deadline, and hold the payment until KYC is satisfied. Do not make an exception for a large or urgent payment, as that would breach the bank's controls.
questions.question: A new customer's payment is blocked because their KYC is incomplete, and they say the payment is urgent. You are the BA handling the case. Why can the payment not go ahead, and what do you ask the customer to do?

questions.answer: Check the alert against the customer's normal behaviour, such as the usual amount, frequency and beneficiary, and gather the supporting documents before deciding. If the activity is explained, close the alert with the evidence; if it is not explained, escalate it to the AML team for further review. Do not dismiss an alert just because the customer is long-standing, as that is when unusual activity is most easily missed.
questions.question: Transaction monitoring flags a long-standing customer's payment as unusual because it is far larger than their normal payments. You are the BA reviewing the alert. How do you decide whether to close it or escalate it?

questions.answer: Apply the strictest applicable list, because a payment can be subject to more than one sanctions regime depending on the currency, the corridor and the parties involved. Check OFAC, EU and UN lists, and escalate to compliance if they conflict or if any list hits. Do not choose the most convenient list, as that could breach the stricter regime.
questions.question: A payment is clear under one sanctions list but hits another, and the team is unsure which list applies. You are the BA deciding the case. How do you resolve the conflict, and who do you escalate to?

questions.answer: Escalate the payment to compliance for enhanced due diligence, because dual-use goods can be used for both civilian and military purposes and a high-risk corridor increases the risk. Ask the customer for the end-user, the purpose and the supporting documents, and do not release the payment until compliance is satisfied. Record the decision and the evidence, so the bank can show it checked the payment properly.
questions.question: A trade payment is for dual-use goods to a high-risk corridor, and the sales team wants it processed quickly. You are the BA reviewing the payment. What extra checks do you require, and why?

questions.answer: Show the regulator the full audit trail: the payment instruction, the screening result, the list version used, the decision, the person who made it, and the timestamp. If any part of the trail is missing, treat it as a control gap and fix the logging, rather than reconstructing it from memory. A complete trail proves the bank screened the payment at the time, not just that it can explain it now.
questions.question: A regulator asks you to prove that a specific payment was screened for sanctions at the time it was made. You are the BA producing the evidence. What must the audit trail show, and what do you do if part of it is missing?

questions.answer: File the report through the proper channel and do not tell the customer that a report has been filed, because that could be tipping off and could prejudice an investigation. Record the facts, the amounts and the dates, and let the compliance team decide whether a report is required. Give the customer only a neutral update that their payment is under review, without revealing the suspicion.
questions.question: You suspect a payment may be linked to money laundering and the customer asks why their payment is delayed. You are the BA handling the case. What do you report, and what must you not tell the customer?

questions.answer: Tell the merchant that storing full card numbers breaches PCI-DSS and creates a serious data-breach risk, and that the cost of a breach far outweighs the convenience. Offer tokenisation or a compliant provider that stores the card securely, so the merchant never sees the full number. If they refuse, escalate to compliance and risk, because this is a security requirement, not a business preference.
questions.question: A merchant wants to store customers' full card numbers to speed up repeat orders, and says they will keep the spreadsheet password-protected. You are the BA who has to stop them. What do you say, and what alternative do you offer?

questions.answer: Explain that PSD2 requires strong customer authentication for most electronic payments, usually two factors such as something the customer knows and something they have. Use risk-based exemptions for low-risk transactions, so most customers get a frictionless experience and only higher-risk ones face a challenge. Do not remove authentication for all transactions, as that would breach the regulation and increase fraud.
questions.question: Product wants to remove all authentication steps to make checkout faster, citing PSD2 exemptions. You are the BA setting the authentication policy. What does PSD2 actually require, and where can you use exemptions?

questions.answer: Tell the customer their payment is under review, give them a realistic timescale, and offer to update them by a specific date, without disclosing that it is a compliance or sanctions check. Keep the language neutral and empathetic, and do not promise a release date you cannot guarantee. Escalate the case to compliance with the customer's details, so the review is completed as quickly as possible.
questions.question: A customer's payment is on a compliance hold and they are angry, demanding to know why. You are the BA on the call. How do you handle the hold without upsetting them further, and what must you not disclose?

questions.answer: Screen the beneficiary name, address, account details and any other identifiers against the sanctions lists, using fuzzy matching to catch spelling variations. If there is a hit, hold the payment and escalate to compliance; if it is a false positive, record the decision and release it. Do not screen on name alone, as that creates too many false positives and misses real matches on other identifiers.
questions.question: A payment is to a beneficiary whose name is spelled slightly differently from a listed name. You are the BA designing the screening check. What do you screen, and how do you decide whether it is a hit or a false positive?

questions.answer: Agree a clear release process with compliance: a false positive is released once the identifiers are checked and the decision is recorded, within a defined SLA. Track the false-positive rate and the time to release, and tune the matching rules if the rate is too high. Do not let false positives sit in a queue with no owner, as that is what turns a routine check into a customer complaint.
questions.question: False-positive sanctions hits are taking days to release and customers are complaining. You are the BA fixing the process. What release process and SLA do you propose, and how do you reduce the false-positive rate?

questions.answer: Apply enhanced due diligence for the corridor: ask for the source of funds, the purpose of the payment, and the beneficiary's details, and check the payment against the sanctions and AML lists. Do not process the payment on the basis of the customer's word alone, and record the checks and the decision. If the customer cannot provide the information, hold the payment and escalate to compliance.
questions.question: A customer wants to send a remittance through a high-risk corridor and cannot explain the source of the funds. You are the BA reviewing the payment. What enhanced checks do you require, and when do you refuse to process it?

questions.answer: Ask the customer for evidence of the source of funds, such as a salary slip, a sale agreement or a business invoice, and compare it with the payment amount and frequency. If the evidence explains the payment, record it and proceed; if it does not, escalate to the AML team. Do not accept a vague explanation such as savings without supporting documents for a large or unusual payment.
questions.question: A customer receives a large payment and cannot explain where the money came from, saying only that it is savings. You are the BA handling the case. What evidence do you ask for, and what do you do if they cannot provide it?

questions.answer: Block the payment, because routing through an intermediary does not remove the sanctions risk, and the bank is still responsible for the payment. Escalate to compliance with the full payment route, the beneficiary and the intermediary details. Do not process the payment on the basis that the intermediary will handle the check, as the bank must do its own screening.
questions.question: A payment is to a sanctioned country, routed through an intermediary in another country, and the sender says the intermediary will handle the checks. You are the BA reviewing the payment. Why is that not acceptable, and what do you do?

questions.answer: Apply enhanced due diligence for a politically exposed person, including checking the source of wealth, the purpose of the account, and ongoing monitoring of their transactions. Do not refuse the customer solely because they are a PEP, but do apply the extra checks and get senior approval. Record the PEP status and the checks, so the bank can show it managed the higher risk.
questions.question: A new customer is a politically exposed person and the team is unsure whether to accept them. You are the BA advising on the onboarding. What extra checks apply, and when would you accept them?

questions.answer: Look for the pattern, such as many small payments in and one large payment out, or payments from many different people to one account with no clear purpose. Escalate the pattern to the fraud and AML teams with the evidence, and do not warn the account holder. Freeze or block the account only on compliance instruction, and record the decision and the evidence.
questions.question: You notice an account receiving many small payments from different people and sending one large payment out, with no clear purpose. You are the BA who spots a possible money-mule pattern. What do you do, and what must you not do?

questions.answer: Screen the entity, its beneficial owners and any related vessels or addresses, not just the company name, because a sanctioned person can control an entity through ownership. If a beneficial owner is sanctioned, escalate to compliance and hold the payment. Do not process the payment on the basis that the company name itself is clear, as the ownership is what matters.
questions.question: A payment is to a company whose name is clear, but one of its beneficial owners is on a sanctions list. You are the BA reviewing the payment. Why does the ownership matter, and what do you do?

questions.answer: Re-screen the payment against the updated list, because a payment that was clear yesterday may hit today if the list has changed. Hold the payment until the re-screening is complete, and record the list version used for each check. Do not rely on yesterday's screening result, as the bank must use the current list at the time of execution.
questions.question: A payment was screened yesterday and was clear, but the sanctions list is updated overnight and the payment has not yet been executed. You are the BA on the morning shift. Do you re-screen it, and why?

questions.answer: Look at the customer's activity across all their accounts, because structuring can be split across accounts to avoid detection in any single one. Escalate the combined pattern to the AML team with the total amount and the dates, and do not warn the customer. Record the pattern across accounts, so the investigation is not limited to one account.
questions.question: A customer is making payments just below a threshold, split across three different accounts they hold. Each account on its own looks normal. You are the BA who spots the combined pattern. What do you do?

questions.answer: Explain that the hold is a legal requirement and cannot be lifted to meet a payroll deadline, and offer to help the customer with an alternative, such as a payment from another account once compliance is satisfied. Escalate the case to compliance with the payroll deadline, so it is prioritised, and give the customer a realistic timescale. Do not promise a release time you cannot guarantee.
questions.question: A business customer's payroll payment is on a compliance hold and their staff will not be paid on time. The business owner demands the hold be lifted. You are the BA handling the case. What do you tell them, and what do you do behind the scenes?

questions.answer: Stop the logging of full card numbers immediately, because card data in logs breaches PCI-DSS and creates a serious breach risk if the logs are accessed. Work with engineering to mask or tokenise the card number in logs, and delete any historical logs that contain full numbers. Report the issue to compliance and risk, and review what other sensitive data may be in the logs.
questions.question: You discover full card numbers are being written to application logs during a project review. You are the BA who finds it. What do you do first, and why is this a PCI-DSS problem?

questions.answer: Check whether the step-up failed because of a technical issue, such as a broken app redirect, or because the customer failed the authentication, and fix the technical issue first. Offer the customer an alternative authentication method, such as a one-time code, and do not disable strong customer authentication to let them through. Record the failure so the authentication experience can be improved.
questions.question: A customer is locked out because the strong customer authentication step keeps failing, and they cannot make a payment. You are the BA handling the complaint. How do you help them without weakening the authentication?

questions.answer: Escalate the missed deadline immediately to compliance, explain the cause, and file the report as soon as possible with a note about the delay. Do not backdate the report or hide the miss, as that creates a bigger regulatory problem. Fix the process so the deadline is tracked with an alert well before it expires, rather than relying on a single person to remember it.
questions.question: A regulatory report is due today and your team realises it will be missed. You are the BA who discovers the miss. What do you do, and what must you not do to cover it up?

questions.answer: Ask for an end-user certificate and supporting documents that show who will use the goods and for what purpose, and escalate to compliance for a decision. Do not process the payment on the basis of the sales team's assurance alone, as the bank needs evidence of the end use. If the documents are not provided, hold the payment and explain to the customer what is needed.
questions.question: A trade payment is for goods that could be used for military purposes, and the customer cannot provide an end-user certificate. You are the BA reviewing the payment. What do you ask for, and when do you refuse to process it?

questions.answer: Apply enhanced due diligence even for a charity, because a high-risk corridor and a charity can still be misused, and the bank must check the charity's registration, purpose and beneficiaries. Ask for the charity's documents and the purpose of the payment, and record the checks. Do not exempt the payment from checks solely because it is for a good cause.
questions.question: A charity wants to send money through a high-risk corridor and asks for the checks to be waived because it is for a good cause. You are the BA reviewing the payment. Why do you still apply enhanced checks, and what do you ask for?

questions.answer: Retain the screening logs for the period required by the bank's policy and the regulator, with the list version, the result, the decision and the timestamp for each payment. If a log is missing, treat it as a control gap and fix the retention, rather than recreating it from memory. Show the auditor the retention policy and a sample of logs, so they can see the process is consistent.
questions.question: An auditor asks how long you keep sanctions screening logs and whether you can show the log for a payment from six months ago. You are the BA answering. What must you be able to show, and what if a log is missing?

questions.answer: Escalate the payment to compliance, because a payment to a sanctioned country is high risk even if it is for family support, and there may be a humanitarian exemption or a licence that applies. Do not process it on the basis of the customer's explanation alone, and do not promise that it will be allowed. Give the customer a clear explanation of the review and a timescale, and let compliance decide whether an exemption applies.
questions.question: A customer wants to send money to family in a sanctioned country and says it is only for living expenses. You are the BA handling the request. Why can you not approve it on the spot, and what do you do?

questions.answer: Check the payment against the bank's crypto policy and the transaction monitoring rules, because some crypto-related payments are high risk or prohibited. Escalate any payment that does not fit the policy to compliance, and do not process it on the basis that the customer says it is legitimate. Record the payment's purpose and the counterparty, so the bank can show it checked the risk.
questions.question: A customer is sending payments to a crypto exchange and transaction monitoring flags them as unusual. You are the BA reviewing the alerts. How do you decide whether to allow the payments, and what do you check?

questions.answer: Explain that KYC must be refreshed periodically and when the customer's circumstances change, even if they have been a customer for years, because the bank must keep its records up to date. Ask for the updated documents, give a clear deadline, and hold the payment until the refresh is complete. Offer to help the customer provide the documents, but do not make an exception that would breach the bank's policy.
questions.question: A customer who has banked with you for ten years has a payment blocked because their KYC needs refreshing, and they say they have already proved who they are. You are the BA explaining the refresh. Why is it needed, and what do you ask them to do?

questions.answer: Explain that screening requires sharing certain payment details with the screening system, but only the minimum necessary, and that the bank's privacy notice covers this use. Do not share more data than the screening needs, and do not use the screening data for marketing or other purposes. If a customer objects, escalate to compliance and the data protection team, rather than turning off the screening.
questions.question: A customer objects to their payment details being screened, saying it breaches their privacy. You are the BA handling the objection. How do you balance data privacy with the legal duty to screen payments?

questions.answer: Apply the 50 percent rule: if a sanctioned person owns 50 percent or more of an entity, directly or indirectly, the entity is treated as sanctioned even if it is not listed by name. Check the ownership structure, add up the sanctioned ownership, and escalate to compliance if it reaches the threshold. Do not process the payment on the basis that the entity's name is clear, as the ownership is what triggers the rule.
questions.question: A payment is to an entity that is not listed, but a sanctioned person owns 60 percent of it. A colleague says the payment is fine because the entity itself is not on the list. You are the BA correcting them. Why are they wrong, and what do you do?

questions.answer: Check the invoice against the market price, the goods and the payment amount, because over- or under-invoicing can be used to move money illicitly. Ask for the contract, the shipping documents and the price evidence, and escalate to the AML team if the price does not make sense. Do not process the payment on the basis of the invoice alone, as the invoice itself may be the problem.
questions.question: A trade payment is for goods invoiced at three times the market price, and the sales team says it is just a premium product. You are the BA reviewing the payment. What do you check, and when do you escalate it?

questions.answer: Do not tell the customer it is a sanctions check, because that could be tipping off and could prejudice an investigation, and it may also be inaccurate if the hold is for another compliance reason. Use neutral language, such as the payment is under review, give a timescale, and offer to update them. Let compliance decide what, if anything, can be disclosed once the review is complete.
questions.question: A stakeholder wants support to tell a customer exactly why their payment is on hold, saying honesty is better. You are the BA who has to refuse. Why must support not disclose the specific compliance reason?

questions.answer: Act immediately: find out what data was breached, whether your customers' card data was affected, and what the processor has done to contain it. Notify compliance, risk and affected customers as required, and review whether to continue using the processor. Do not wait for the processor to tell you the full story, as the bank remains responsible for its customers' data.
questions.question: Your third-party card processor suffers a data breach and you do not know whether your customers' card data was affected. You are the BA on the incident. What do you do first, and who do you notify?

questions.answer: Explain that open banking requires the customer's explicit consent for a third party to access their account or initiate a payment, and that consent must be specific, informed and revocable. Check that the consent covers the exact payment and the third party, and do not process a payment where consent is missing or has expired. Tell the customer how to review and revoke their consent, so they stay in control.
questions.question: A third party wants to initiate a payment from a customer's account under open banking, but the customer is unsure what they consented to. You are the BA explaining the consent. What must the consent cover, and what do you do if it is unclear?

questions.answer: Refuse to launch before compliance sign-off, because a new corridor brings new sanctions, AML and regulatory risks that must be assessed first. Present the stakeholder with the compliance checklist, the time needed, and the risk of launching without it, including fines and loss of licence. Agree a launch date that allows compliance to complete its review, rather than launching and fixing the controls afterwards.
questions.question: A stakeholder wants to launch a new payment corridor next week, before compliance has signed it off, to beat a competitor. You are the BA on the project. Why do you refuse, and what launch plan do you propose instead?

questions.answer: I start by observing the current process and measuring where time is actually lost, for example in manual checks, approvals, or batch cut-offs, rather than guessing. I then ask for concrete examples and success measures, such as a target time from instruction to release. Only after that do I write requirements tied to those measures, so the team can prove the change worked.
questions.question: A business stakeholder says 'we just need the payment process to be faster' but cannot explain what is slow. How do you turn that vague ask into workable requirements?

questions.answer: I map both versions side by side and then check them against real cases, system logs, and the people who actually do each step. Differences usually come from exceptions, workarounds, or different teams handling different payment types. I document the agreed as-is process with the exceptions called out, and get both managers to confirm it before I design the to-be.
questions.question: Two operations managers describe the same payment approval process in completely different ways. How do you find out which version is correct?

questions.answer: I use interviews when the topic is sensitive, when I need detail from one expert, or when stakeholders disagree and need space to speak honestly. I use a workshop when I need a shared decision, to resolve conflicts in the room, or to map a process that crosses several teams. Often I do interviews first to understand the issues, then a workshop to agree the outcome.
questions.question: You are the BA on a payments project where one expert holds sensitive pricing knowledge and three teams disagree loudly in meetings. How do you decide when to use one-to-one interviews and when to use a workshop?

questions.answer: I find out why they are cancelling, then offer a shorter format that fits, such as a 30-minute focused review of a draft instead of a two-hour workshop. I send the draft in advance with clear questions, so the meeting is a decision point, not a blank page. If they still cannot attend, I agree a named delegate who can decide on their behalf and record that in writing.
questions.question: A senior stakeholder keeps cancelling your requirements workshops. How do you still get the input you need without delaying the project?

questions.answer: I trace one real payment from start to finish, noting who touches it, which systems it passes through, and what can go wrong at each step. I use that walkthrough to ask targeted questions instead of open-ended ones. Then I draft the flow with the gaps marked clearly, so stakeholders can correct a concrete document rather than invent a process from scratch.
questions.question: You are asked to write requirements for a new payment type, but the business cannot describe the full end-to-end flow. What do you do first?

questions.answer: I put the business problem, objectives, scope, and success measures in the BRD, because that is what business sign-off is about. The FRD holds the detailed system behaviour, rules, fields, and validations the developers and testers need. User stories work best for iterative delivery, where each story is a small slice of value with acceptance criteria, and the BRD and FRD give the overall context behind them.
questions.question: You are the BA on a project where the sponsor wants a BRD, the developers want user stories, and the testers want an FRD, all for the same payment feature. How do you decide what goes where without duplicating everything three times?

questions.answer: I add the missing specifics the developer actually needs: the exact fields, the business rules, the valid and invalid values, and what happens in the error cases. I write acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then form so the expected behaviour is testable. Then I walk through one example with the developer to check my understanding before they start building.
questions.question: A developer says your user story is too vague to build. What do you add to make it usable without writing a full specification?

questions.answer: Given a payment above the threshold is submitted, when the first approver approves it, then it moves to pending second approval and is not released. Given the second approver approves it, when approval is complete, then the payment is released for processing. Given the second approver rejects it, when the rejection is recorded, then the payment is returned to the maker with the reason shown and no release happens.
questions.question: You are the BA on a project where a payment over a set threshold must need a second approver before it is released. Write the acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then form.

questions.answer: I ask what happens if each item is not delivered, because a true Must is something the product cannot launch without, such as a regulatory or safety control. I make the trade-offs visible by showing time, cost, and risk for each item, and I get the group to agree the cut line together. If everything still looks like a Must, I ask them to rank the Musts, so at least the build order is agreed.
questions.question: A stakeholder insists every feature is 'must have'. How do you run a MoSCoW prioritisation that actually produces a decision?

questions.answer: I first assess the impact: the new currency affects fields, validations, exchange-rate handling, testing, and possibly downstream systems. I present that impact and the options, such as adding it now and dropping something else, or scheduling it for the next sprint. I do not let the change slip in silently; it goes through change control, is documented, and the product owner decides with the full cost visible.
questions.question: Mid-sprint, the business asks to add a new currency to a payment screen that is already in development. How do you handle the change?

questions.answer: Scope creep is an unapproved addition that quietly grows the work, while a genuine change is a recognised new need that goes through impact assessment and approval. For creep I point back to the agreed scope and ask for a formal change request. For a genuine change I assess cost, time, and risk, update the documents and traceability, and get sign-off before the team builds it.
questions.question: You are the BA on a project where the business keeps asking for 'just one more small thing' every week. How do you tell whether each ask is scope creep or a genuine change, and what do you do about each?

questions.answer: Traceability lets me follow the chain from the business need to the requirement, the design, the code, and the test case, so I can see exactly where the meaning changed. I check whether the requirement was unclear, the design misread it, or the build drifted from the design. Then I fix the right link in the chain and update the affected documents, rather than patching the symptom.
questions.question: A requirement was signed off, then a tester finds the built feature behaves differently. How does traceability help you resolve this?

questions.answer: I start from the live requirements and work backwards to the business objectives and forwards to the test cases, filling the matrix as I go. I focus first on high-risk areas such as sanctions screening, limits, and settlement, where a missed link matters most. I build it incrementally alongside current work and share it early, so the team can correct it while it is still useful.
questions.question: You are the BA joining a payments project halfway through and there is no traceability matrix. How do you build one without stopping delivery?

questions.answer: I map the current system's functions, fields, rules, and reports, then map the new platform's capabilities against the same list. Each item is marked as covered, partly covered, or missing, with the business impact of every gap noted. The gaps then become decisions: change the process, configure or customise the new system, or accept the gap with a workaround.
questions.question: You are the BA on a bank project replacing a legacy payment system with a new platform, and the vendor claims the new system 'does everything the old one does'. How do you prove or disprove that claim before the bank commits?

questions.answer: I first understand why each workaround exists, because it usually fills a real gap in the system or a rule that no longer fits. I take each one to the process owners and ask whether the to-be system should handle it properly, whether the rule should change, or whether the workaround can be removed. I never design a to-be that silently assumes the workarounds will disappear.
questions.question: You are the BA and your as-is process map shows five manual workarounds that nobody had mentioned. How do you handle them in the to-be design?

questions.answer: I write the current state first, with volumes, times, failure points, and pain points backed by evidence such as logs or incident counts. Then I describe the target state in the same terms, so the improvement is measurable rather than a slogan. Finally I list the changes needed to get from one to the other, with the owner and the risk for each change, so the business can see what the to-be actually costs.
questions.question: You are the BA asked to present as-is versus to-be process maps to senior managers who must approve funding for a payment redesign. How do you make the maps drive that decision instead of just looking impressive?

questions.answer: I capture the obvious ones such as response time and availability, but I also check audit trails, data retention, security, recoverability, and how the system behaves at peak volume. For payments I confirm the exact service-level targets, for example the maximum time to process a payment at month-end volume, and how failures are detected and reported. I then write acceptance criteria for each non-functional requirement so it can be tested, not just stated.
questions.question: A business user gives you functional requirements for a new payment service but nothing non-functional. What do you elicit, and why does it matter for payments?

questions.answer: I ask for the audit evidence: every state change, who made it, when, and the before and after values, with the trail being tamper-evident and retained for the required period. I check what reports operations and compliance need, and how often they need them. Then I write the audit requirement as specific fields and events, not as a general statement like 'the system must be auditable'.
questions.question: You are the BA and compliance says a payment system must be 'fully auditable'. How do you turn that into testable requirements?

questions.answer: I bring both stakeholders together with the same facts: the impact on time, risk, cost, and customers of each option. I ask what outcome each side is really trying to protect, because the surface disagreement often hides a shared goal. If they still cannot agree, I present the options with a recommendation to the decision owner, and I record the decision and its reasons so it is not reopened later.
questions.question: You are the BA and operations wants same-day settlement for all payments, but risk wants extra checks that slow it down. How do you handle these conflicting requirements?

questions.answer: I list each requirement with its source, its priority, and its dependency, then highlight the conflicts explicitly instead of burying them. I ask each stakeholder to explain the business reason behind their requirement, and I look for a compromise such as phased delivery or different treatment for different payment types. Unresolved conflicts go to the decision owner with the impact of each option spelled out.
questions.question: You are the BA and you receive requirements from three teams and several directly contradict each other. What is your process for resolving them?

questions.answer: I start by defining what a successful migration looks like: which payment types move, which customers are affected, and what must still work on day one. I map every field, rule, and status from the old system to the new one, and I identify the gaps and the data that needs cleansing. I also plan for parallel running, cutover, and rollback, because migration requirements are not just about the new system but about the move itself.
questions.question: You are asked to write requirements for a payments migration from one platform to another. Where do you start, and what do you include that a normal feature would not need?

questions.answer: I first confirm whether the flow is a business rule or a technical limit, and what would break if it changed. If it is a business rule, I find its owner and ask what risk it controls, then look for a safer alternative such as an additional check. If it is a technical limit, I work with the developers on the cost of removing it. I never quietly write a requirement around an unexplained constraint.
questions.question: During migration discovery you find the old system has a hard-coded limit that nobody can explain. How do you handle it in the requirements?

questions.answer: I draw the flow from instruction to settlement, showing each system, the message or file passed, and the data at each step. I keep the business view simple and put the field-level detail in a mapping document linked to each step. I validate it by walking a real payment through it with operations and technology, checking the happy path and the main exceptions.
questions.question: You are the BA on a payment project where business users say your flow document is too technical and developers say it is too vague. How do you document the flow so both sides can actually use the same document?

questions.answer: I list every source field and target field with its format, length, mandatory status, and transformation rule, plus an example value. I include the rules for missing or invalid data and what the system must do in each case. I test the mapping with real examples, including edge cases such as a missing beneficiary address, before the build starts.
questions.question: You are the BA mapping fields from a legacy payment file to a new ISO 20022 message, and you discover the old file has no field for the beneficiary address the new message requires. What does your mapping document need to cover, and how do you resolve the gap?

questions.answer: I check whether the change affects the payment's meaning, such as the amount, currency, beneficiary, or value date, or only its presentation. Meaningful changes need re-approval from the affected business owners and a retest of the impacted cases. Cosmetic changes can be noted and approved by the product owner. I record the decision in the change log so the sign-off remains accurate.
questions.question: After sign-off, the business asks for a small change to a payment screen. How do you decide whether the signed-off requirements need formal re-approval?

questions.answer: I send the document early, highlight what has changed since the last review, and ask reviewers to raise issues before the meeting. In the meeting I walk through the decisions, not the whole document, and I capture any open points with an owner and a date. Sign-off is a clear written confirmation that the scope and the rules are agreed, not a silent absence of objections.
questions.question: You are the BA running a sign-off review and you suspect stakeholders will just rubber-stamp the requirements without reading them. How do you get a meaningful approval instead?

questions.answer: I go back to the person who raised it with the evidence: the signed-off scope, the cost and risk of the change, and the effect on the delivery date. I offer options, such as deferring it to the next release or swapping it for a lower-priority item. If they still push for it, I ask them to raise a formal change request so the decision is visible and owned.
questions.question: A stakeholder says after sign-off, 'I thought this was included.' How do you respond without damaging the relationship or silently accepting extra work?

questions.answer: I check first whether the missing requirement is a real gap or a misunderstanding of what is already covered. If it is a real gap, I write it up with its business impact and test it against the original objectives. Then I take it through change control, because adding it after sign-off changes the baseline and the team needs to know the cost.
questions.question: During build, the team finds a requirement that was missed at sign-off. What is your process for adding it?

questions.answer: I use the requirements to write the happy path, then deliberately add the failure cases: invalid data, missing data, timeouts, duplicates, and system outages. I ask operations what goes wrong most often in production and turn those incidents into scenarios. I review the scenarios with testers before testing starts, so gaps are found early.
questions.question: You are the BA reviewing requirements for a new payment feature and every scenario is a happy path. A payment fails in production on day one because nobody covered the failure cases. What would you have done differently, and how do you fix the coverage now?

questions.answer: I ask the business to show me the rule in action with real examples, including the cases that are just inside and just outside the limit. I write the rule with its thresholds, its exceptions, and the action for each outcome, and I check it with compliance or risk if the rule is regulatory. Then I add test cases for each boundary so the rule is verified, not assumed.
questions.question: A business rule says 'high-value payments need extra checks'. How do you turn that into a precise, testable requirement?

questions.answer: I start by confirming what 'faster' and 'same-day' mean in measurable terms, such as the time from instruction to release for each payment type. I map the current steps and find the real delays, which are often approvals, cut-off times, or manual checks rather than system speed. I then propose changes to the steps, checks, or sequencing, and I show the expected time saving for each change.
questions.question: A client asks for same-day payments, but the current process takes two days. How do you analyse the requirement and propose a solution?

questions.answer: I bring the evidence: the requirement as written, the test result, and the business impact of the difference. I ask the developer to explain their interpretation, because the gap is usually an ambiguous phrase or an unstated assumption. We agree the correct behaviour, update the requirement if it was unclear, and record the fix so the same ambiguity does not recur.
questions.question: A developer builds a feature differently from what you wrote, and both of you think you are right. How do you resolve it?

questions.answer: I keep the business language in the requirement and put the technical detail in a linked note, so each audience sees what it needs. I define each technical term once, in plain language, the first time it appears. I also walk through the document with business reviewers using a real example, so they can check the behaviour without needing to understand the technology.
questions.question: You are the BA whose requirements document is full of technical terms, and a business reviewer refuses to sign it because she cannot understand it, while developers say removing the detail makes it unbuildable. How do you resolve the standoff?

questions.answer: I look at the data first: volumes, failure rates, times of day, and which steps take longest. I then talk to the people who handle the exceptions, because they know the real causes. I present the findings as options with the evidence for each, so the business can choose a fix based on facts rather than opinions.
questions.question: You are the BA and operations reports that payment failures have doubled, but nobody knows why. How do you investigate before proposing a fix?

questions.answer: I check the source system, the file format, the mapping rules, and the validation that should have caught the error. I find the first point where the data diverges from the expected value, and I check whether the rule, the mapping, or the source data is at fault. I then fix the root cause and add a check so the same error is caught earlier next time.
questions.question: A payment file fails in production because a field was mapped incorrectly. How do you trace the problem and prevent it happening again?

questions.answer: I first check whether the old rule still serves a purpose, such as a regulatory limit or a fraud control, by asking its original owners and checking incident history. If the rule is obsolete, I document the evidence and get the owner to agree it can be dropped. If it is still needed, I write it as an explicit requirement in the new system instead of letting it survive as an undocumented habit.
questions.question: You are the BA on a migration and you discover the old system enforces a payment limit that no document mentions and nobody can explain. Do you carry the limit into the new system or drop it, and how do you decide?

questions.answer: I ask the sponsor what decision they need to make and by when, then I work backwards to the smallest set of requirements that supports that decision. I mark the rest as later-phase items with owners and dates, and I make clear what the team is assuming in the meantime. I would rather deliver a thin, honest baseline on time than a thick document that arrives after the decision is made.
questions.question: You are the BA on a project where the sponsor needs a signed-off requirements baseline in two weeks, but elicitation will take six. What do you deliver, and how do you handle what is left out?

questions.answer: I treat the workaround as a requirement in disguise: I find out what it achieves, how often it is used, and what breaks if it stops. I then take it to the process owner with options, such as building the capability properly, changing the rule, or keeping a controlled manual step. I record the decision so the to-be design does not silently assume the workaround will vanish.
questions.question: You are the BA mapping a payment process and you find operations staff keep a spreadsheet outside the system to track payments the system cannot. How do you handle that shadow process in your requirements?

questions.answer: I separate the regulatory must-dos from the business nice-to-haves, because the regulator's items cannot be traded away. I then sequence the work so the compliant minimum viable product launches first, with the enhancements in a named later release. I get the regulator-facing owners to confirm the minimum in writing, so the team is not guessing about compliance.
questions.question: You are the BA on a payment product where new regulations arrive mid-project and the deadline cannot move. How do you reprioritise the requirements without breaking compliance or the launch date?

questions.answer: I ask for the evidence behind the claim, such as volumes, error rates, or customer complaints, and I compare it with what the data actually shows. If the evidence supports the change, I write the requirement with the measurable outcome attached. If it does not, I present the data and propose a smaller experiment, so the decision is based on facts rather than the loudest voice.
questions.question: You are the BA in a workshop where a senior manager insists a new payment feature will 'double volumes', but nobody has any data to support it. How do you handle the claim without dismissing the manager?

questions.answer: I first confirm the exact cut-off times, time zones, and value-date rules for each payment type, because 'same day' means different things in different corridors. I then map the steps that must happen before cut-off and find which ones can move earlier or run in parallel. I present the options with the risk of each, such as releasing payments with less checking time, and let the business owner decide.
questions.question: You are the BA on a project where corporate clients want payments released after 4pm to still settle the same day, but the clearing cut-off is 3pm. How do you work through the trade-off?

questions.answer: I run a structured session where each team states its requirement, its reason, and what happens if it is not met. I look for the underlying goal, because two teams often want the same outcome through different means. Where no compromise exists, I escalate with a clear recommendation and the cost of each option, and I record the decision and its owner.
questions.question: You are the BA in a room where operations, compliance, and technology each demand a different payment approval flow and none will budge. How do you get to a decision?

questions.answer: I start with the smallest viable slice, such as one payment type for one customer group, and I define the acceptance criteria for that slice. I then list the dependencies and risks for the rest, so the team knows what 'later' actually means. I make sure the phased plan is agreed in writing, so the first release is not judged as a failure for missing what was always planned for phase two.
questions.question: You are the BA on a payments programme that is too big to deliver in one release, but the sponsor wants everything at once. How do you propose a phased approach that the sponsor will accept?

questions.answer: I check the impact on the payment itself first: amount, currency, beneficiary, and value date are the fields that matter most. I then trace which systems and reports use the field, and which validations depend on it. I write the change with its ripple effects listed, get approval from the affected owners, and make sure the test cases cover the changed field end to end.
questions.question: You are the BA and the business asks to change the format of the beneficiary reference field mid-build. How do you assess whether it is a trivial change or a risky one?

questions.answer: I ask the team to show me the exact rule that is unclear, using a real payment example where the rule gives two different answers. I then go back to the rule owner with that example and ask for the intended outcome, rather than asking them to rewrite the whole rule. I update the requirement with the clarified rule and the example, so the next person does not hit the same ambiguity.
questions.question: You are the BA and a developer tells you a business rule for payment fees is ambiguous because it gives different results for the same payment. How do you get it clarified without a week of meetings?

questions.answer: I look for the requirement that is missing or wrong by comparing the expected behaviour with the actual behaviour for that specific case. I then check whether the gap is in the requirement, the design, or the build, and I fix it at the right level. I also add the missing case to the requirements and the test pack, so the defect becomes a documented rule rather than a one-off fix.
questions.question: You are the BA on a UAT where a tester finds a payment is rejected for a reason nobody documented. How do you decide whether it is a defect, a missing requirement, or correct behaviour?

questions.answer: I define the non-functional targets with the business and technology together, such as the maximum processing time at peak volume and the recovery time after an outage. I write each one with a number and a test method, so it can be verified rather than debated. I also agree what happens if a target is missed, such as degrading gracefully or queueing payments, rather than failing silently.
questions.question: You are the BA on a payment platform that must handle ten times its normal volume on salary day, and the business says it 'just needs to cope'. How do you turn that into requirements the team can build and test against?

questions.answer: I first find out why the sign-off is being withheld: is the requirement wrong, is something missing, or is the reviewer simply overloaded? I address the specific concern with evidence or a change, and I offer a shorter review of just the disputed section. If the delay is about workload, I agree a deadline and a delegate, and I escalate to the sponsor if the project date is at risk.
questions.question: You are the BA and a key approver refuses to sign off your requirements, but will not say exactly what is wrong with them. How do you move forward?

questions.answer: I ask what has changed since sign-off: a new regulation, a new payment type, or a new risk the business has discovered. I then assess the impact of the change on the design, the build, and the test pack, and I present the options with their costs. I update the baseline through change control, so the team is working from one agreed version, not from a series of verbal updates.
questions.question: You are the BA two weeks after sign-off when compliance adds a new sanctions-check requirement that changes the payment flow. How do you bring it into the project without derailing the team?

questions.answer: I map the data needed at each step and find where it is created, transformed, or lost, using real payment examples. I then check which system owns each piece of data and whether the receiving system can use it as-is. I write the data requirements alongside the process requirements, because a flow that looks right on paper fails when the data does not travel with it.
questions.question: You are the BA documenting a payment flow and you realise the beneficiary details entered at the front end never reach the settlement system. How do you find and fix the data gap?

questions.answer: I ask the business to define 'urgent' with examples: which customers, which amounts, and what delay is acceptable. I then design a rule that treats those cases differently, such as a fast-track queue with its own checks, rather than letting every payment claim to be urgent. I write the rule with its limits and its audit trail, so the exception does not become the norm.
questions.question: You are the BA on a project where the business wants an 'urgent payment' option, but cannot define what counts as urgent. How do you design a requirement that will not be abused?

questions.answer: I bring the two versions together with the evidence: the signed-off document, the test results, and the business impact of each interpretation. I ask both sides to explain their reading using a real payment example, which usually reveals the ambiguous phrase. We agree the correct behaviour, update the wording, and I record the decision so the same dispute does not recur.
questions.question: You are the BA in a meeting where the business and the test team disagree about what a requirement means, and each side has a different document to prove it. How do you resolve it?

questions.answer: I ask the customer-facing team for real examples of the complaints, including the payment details and the exact point of failure. I then trace those examples through the process to find the common cause, rather than fixing each complaint separately. I write requirements that address the root cause, with a measure such as a target reduction in complaints, so the fix can be judged.
questions.question: You are the BA asked to fix a payment process that customers keep complaining about, but the complaints all sound different. How do you find the real problem underneath them?

questions.answer: I confirm the regulatory deadline and what evidence the regulator expects, then I work backwards to the requirements that must be delivered first. I separate the items that are legally required from the items that are simply good practice, and I sequence the work so the legal minimum is ready by the deadline. I keep the sponsor informed of the trade-offs in writing, so the decision to defer anything is explicit.
questions.question: You are the BA on a payments project where a new regulation takes effect in three months, but the full solution will take six. How do you plan a compliant interim solution?

questions.answer: I ask each stakeholder to state their top three requirements and the business outcome each one delivers, then I look for the overlaps and the conflicts. I present the combined picture with the trade-offs visible, such as cost, time, and risk, and I ask the group to agree the priorities together. I record the agreed priorities and the reasons, so later challenges can be answered from the record rather than reopened.
questions.question: You are the BA at the end of elicitation with five stakeholders who each gave you a different list of 'top priorities' for the same payment system. How do you produce one agreed priority list?

questions.answer: I start with the people who are affected by the change, who decide on it, who pay for it, and who can block it, using the org chart, the process map, and conversations with the sponsor. I then assess each person's interest and influence, and I record who needs to be consulted, who decides, and who just needs to be informed. I review the list with the sponsor, because the most dangerous stakeholder is usually the one nobody named.
questions.question: You are the BA starting a payments project and the sponsor gives you three names, but you suspect several important people are missing. How do you identify the full stakeholder set?

questions.answer: I first find out why they are resisting: are they losing control, do they distrust the new process, or were they never consulted? I meet them one-to-one, listen to their concerns, and show them the evidence behind the change using their own team's data. I look for a part of the proposal they can shape, so they become a contributor rather than an opponent, and I keep the sponsor informed of the risk.
