questions.question: You are the BA on a project where a powerful operations manager openly opposes your proposed payment process change in every meeting. How do you handle it?

questions.answer: I tell them early, with the new date, the reason, and what is being done about it, rather than letting them discover the delay themselves. I explain the impact on their work in concrete terms, such as which payments or reports will be affected, and I offer options, such as a partial release or a workaround. I then give regular updates, so the delay is a managed fact rather than a recurring surprise.
questions.question: You are the BA and your payment project will miss its go-live date by four weeks. How do you communicate the delay to business users who have already promised the date to their customers?

questions.answer: I agree the purpose and the decisions needed before the meeting, and I send the background material in advance with clear questions. In the room I keep the discussion on the decisions, park side issues with an owner, and summarise the agreed points as we go. I close by confirming who does what by when, and I send the notes the same day so the decisions do not drift.
questions.question: You are the BA running a workshop with twelve stakeholders from five teams who all have different agendas. How do you keep it focused and end with decisions?

questions.answer: I meet operations and compliance separately first, so I understand each side's real concerns before bringing them together. I present the proposal with the risks and controls for each concern, using their own language and examples. I ask for sign-off on the specific controls they own, rather than a blanket approval, and I record any conditions attached to the approval.
questions.question: You are the BA who needs sign-off from both operations and compliance for a new payment flow, but each team wants different controls. How do you get both approvals?

questions.answer: I explain the problem in terms of its business effect, not its technical cause: for example, 'some payments are delayed by a day because the system waits for a confirmation that never arrives'. I use a simple analogy, such as a letter waiting for a reply that was never sent, and I show the options with their cost and risk. I check understanding by asking what decision they need to make, rather than asking if they followed the technical detail.
questions.question: You are the BA explaining to non-technical business users why payments are failing because of a message timeout in the clearing system. How do you make it understandable without misleading them?

questions.answer: I agree a single source of truth for status, such as a weekly note with the same headings, and I set the meeting time to suit the furthest time zone rather than my own. I record decisions in writing immediately, so nobody has to rely on a meeting they attended at midnight. I also build in overlap time for urgent issues, and I name a contact in each region so questions do not wait a full day.
questions.question: You are the BA working with stakeholders in London, Mumbai, and Singapore, and decisions keep getting lost between time zones. How do you manage expectations and keep everyone aligned?

questions.answer: I first try to resolve it at my level with the facts and the options, giving the other party a clear deadline. If that fails, I escalate with a short summary of the issue, the impact, the options tried, and the decision I need, so the person I escalate to can decide quickly. I tell the other party I am escalating and why, so it is a transparent step rather than a surprise.
questions.question: You are the BA and a development lead has missed three deadlines for a payment feature, and the business is asking you why. When do you escalate, and how do you do it without damaging the working relationship?

questions.answer: I present the findings in the order the managers care about: the decision needed, the options, the evidence, and the recommendation. I use one page of summary with the detail behind it, and I use real numbers, such as volumes and failure rates, rather than adjectives. I also name the risks of doing nothing, so the choice is between options rather than between acting and waiting.
questions.question: You are the BA presenting your findings to senior managers who have ten minutes and want a decision. How do you structure the presentation?

questions.answer: I find out what the other team cares about and frame the request in terms of their goals, not mine. I bring evidence, such as the impact on their customers or their workload, and I offer something in return, such as help with their own priority or a phased approach that reduces their effort. I build the relationship before I need the favour, so the ask is not the first conversation.
questions.question: You are the BA who needs the technology team to prioritise your payment fix, but you have no authority over them and their backlog is full. How do you influence them?

questions.answer: I ask the stakeholder what they need the system to do, using a real payment example, and I write down their words before I offer my interpretation. I then play back my understanding and ask them to correct it, which usually surfaces the real requirement. I also test my understanding with the team who will build it, so any gap is found before the document is signed.
questions.question: You are the BA and a stakeholder keeps saying 'you know what I mean' instead of explaining what they actually want. How do you get a clear requirement out of them?

questions.answer: I prepare a short summary of the issue, the options, the recommendation, and the decision needed, and I send it before the meeting. In the meeting I keep the discussion on the decision, and I make sure the quieter stakeholders are asked directly for their view. I record the decision, the reasons, and the dissenting views, so the outcome is clear even to those who disagreed.
questions.question: You are the BA chairing a meeting where two senior stakeholders disagree in front of everyone and the room goes silent. How do you handle it and still reach a decision?

questions.answer: I acknowledge the concern directly and ask what specifically worries them, because 'the system will fail' usually hides a real risk I can address. I show the evidence, such as test results or a phased rollout plan, and I agree a mitigation, such as parallel running or a rollback plan. I also agree what success looks like after go-live, so the fear can be tested against reality.
questions.question: You are the BA and a business user refuses to accept a new payment system because they are convinced it will fail on day one. How do you win their trust?

questions.answer: I ask the stakeholder to explain the change in their own words and to show me an example of what they want, because the misunderstanding is usually in the detail. I then update the document with the corrected understanding and ask them to confirm it in writing. I also add the example to the requirements, so the next reader sees the intent, not just the words.
questions.question: You are the BA and a stakeholder claims you misunderstood their requirement, but you wrote down exactly what they said in the workshop. How do you resolve the dispute?

questions.answer: I tell the sponsor the truth about the risk, with the evidence and the options, rather than hiding it to keep the meeting pleasant. I frame it as a choice: proceed and accept the risk, delay and reduce it, or change the scope to avoid it. I record the decision and its owner, so the risk is owned rather than silently carried by the team.
questions.question: You are the BA who discovers a serious risk to a payment launch, but the sponsor is under pressure to hit the date and does not want to hear bad news. How do you communicate it?

questions.answer: I start by finding out what the team actually needs from me: the decision, the information, or the escalation. I then set a clear cadence, such as a short daily note during a critical phase, and I keep it consistent so people know when to expect updates. I also check whether my updates are being read and acted on, and I adjust the format if they are not.
questions.question: You are the BA on a project where stakeholders complain they never know what is happening, while the team says they are drowning in status meetings. How do you fix the communication?

questions.answer: I go back to the stakeholder with the draft and ask them to mark the parts that are wrong or missing, rather than defending the whole document. I focus on the specific gaps they raise, fix them with evidence, and ask for confirmation of the corrected sections. If the objection is about scope rather than accuracy, I take it through change control so the decision is explicit.
questions.question: You are the BA and a stakeholder rejects your requirements document outright, saying 'this is not what we asked for'. What do you do next?

questions.answer: I ask the quiet stakeholder for their view directly, in a one-to-one if the group setting silences them, because their silence often hides the most useful knowledge. I then bring their point into the group with the evidence behind it, so it is judged on merit rather than on who said it. I make sure the decision record notes their contribution, so they see that speaking up had an effect.
questions.question: You are the BA in a workshop where one person does all the talking and the quietest person in the room is the one who actually runs the payment process. How do you get their input?

questions.answer: I ask for the data behind the request, such as the volumes or the customer impact, and I compare it with the data for the current priorities. I then present the trade-off: what would be delayed or dropped if this request jumps the queue, and who owns that decision. I offer a compromise, such as a small investigation first, so the stakeholder feels heard without the plan being overturned.
questions.question: You are the BA and a senior stakeholder demands their payment feature be built first, even though it was agreed as low priority last month. How do you handle the request?

questions.answer: I first understand the change and its impact on the people affected, then I tell them before the change happens, not after. I explain what is changing, why, and what they need to do differently, using their own examples. I also name a contact for questions and a date for a review, so the change is a supported transition rather than an announcement.
questions.question: You are the BA on a project where a payment process change will affect 200 operations staff who have not been consulted. How do you communicate the change to them?

questions.answer: I separate the person's style from the substance of their objection, and I respond to the substance with facts and options. I keep the conversation in private where possible, and I record the agreed points in writing so the discussion cannot be rewritten later. If the behaviour continues, I raise it with the sponsor with specific examples and the impact on the project.
questions.question: You are the BA and a stakeholder is rude and dismissive in meetings, but their approval is essential for your payment project. How do you work with them?

questions.answer: I check the facts first: what was actually agreed, when, and by whom, using the meeting notes and the signed-off document. I then present the evidence calmly and ask the stakeholder to show their version, because the gap is usually a misunderstanding rather than a deliberate change. We agree the correct position and record it, so the project moves forward on one version of the truth.
questions.question: You are the BA and a stakeholder denies agreeing to a requirement that you have in writing from them. How do you handle it without accusing them of lying?

questions.answer: I ask the sponsor what decision they need and what information they are missing, then I provide exactly that, with the options and the risks. I avoid technical detail unless they ask for it, and I use the language of cost, time, and customer impact. I also give them a clear recommendation, because a sponsor who has to choose between options without a recommendation is being asked to do the BA's job.
questions.question: You are the BA and your sponsor asks for a five-minute update on a complex payments project. What do you tell them, and what do you leave out?

questions.answer: I find out what each team is actually worried about, because the conflict is often about different risks rather than different facts. I bring the teams together with the shared goal, such as getting payments to customers on time, and I show how each team's requirement affects that goal. I then propose a solution that addresses both risks, or I escalate with the trade-offs clearly stated.
questions.question: You are the BA caught between the compliance team, who want more checks, and the customer team, who want faster payments. Both say the other side does not understand the business. How do you mediate?

questions.answer: I tell the business the truth as soon as I know it, with the reason, the impact, and the options, rather than waiting until the deadline passes. I explain what the team is doing to recover time and what the business can do to help, such as deciding on scope. I then give regular updates against the recovery plan, so the business can plan around the new date.
questions.question: You are the BA and a key payment feature will not be ready for the launch the business has already announced to customers. How do you break the news?

questions.answer: I ask the stakeholder to show me the report or the payment that is wrong, and I trace it back to the source data and the rule that produced it. I then explain the cause in plain language, show the fix, and agree how it will be verified. I also check whether the same error affects other reports, so the fix is complete rather than a single correction.
questions.question: You are the BA and a business user says your new payment report is wrong, but the system is producing exactly what the requirements asked for. How do you respond?

questions.answer: I prepare by understanding the audience's concerns and the decisions they need to make, then I rehearse the key points with a colleague. During the presentation I lead with the recommendation, support it with two or three pieces of evidence, and invite questions early so the audience feels heard. If I do not know an answer, I say so and commit to a date for it, rather than guessing.
questions.question: You are the BA presenting a controversial payment change to a room of senior managers who are known to challenge presenters hard. How do you prepare and handle the challenge?

questions.answer: I ask the stakeholder what outcome they want and what would convince them, then I show them the evidence against that test. If the evidence supports the change, I present it with the risks and the mitigations. If it does not, I say so and propose an alternative, because a BA who only argues for their own proposal loses credibility fast.
questions.question: You are the BA and a stakeholder insists on a payment solution that you believe will not work. How do you persuade them without simply saying 'you are wrong'?

questions.answer: I give the team the information they need to decide, then I step back and let them own the decision, recording it with the reasons. I make sure the decision is written down with its owner and its date, so it cannot be revisited without new evidence. I also check in after the decision to see whether it is working, rather than assuming it was right.
questions.question: You are the BA in a project where the team cannot decide between two payment designs and keeps asking you to choose. How do you help them decide without taking the decision away from them?

questions.answer: I ask the stakeholder to explain the impact of the delay on their work, so I understand what is really at stake. I then give a realistic date based on the team's actual progress, not the date they want to hear, and I explain what would have to change to bring it forward. I follow up with a written update when the date changes, so the stakeholder is never surprised.
questions.question: You are the BA and a stakeholder keeps asking for a delivery date you cannot give yet, because the requirements are still unclear. How do you manage their expectation?

questions.answer: I find a common goal that both teams share, such as reducing payment failures, and I frame the joint work around that goal. I agree clear roles and a single plan, so neither team feels it is doing the other's work. I also celebrate the joint wins, so the collaboration is visible and worth repeating.
questions.question: You are the BA asked to get two teams who have never worked together to jointly design a new payment process. How do you build the collaboration?

questions.answer: I acknowledge the mistake, explain what went wrong and what I am doing to fix it, and give a realistic date for the correction. I do not blame the team or the system, because the stakeholder trusted my document. I then check the corrected document with the stakeholder before it goes wider, so the fix restores confidence rather than just correcting a line.
questions.question: You are the BA and a stakeholder finds an error in a document you sent to senior management. How do you recover credibility?

questions.answer: I ask the stakeholder what information they need and when they need it, then I deliver it in that form, even if it is not my usual format. I keep the updates short and regular, so they do not have to chase me. I also check whether the updates are useful and adjust them, because communication that is ignored is not communication.
questions.question: You are the BA working with a stakeholder who never reads your emails but complains they are never told anything. How do you keep them informed?

questions.answer: I listen to the objection fully before responding, because interrupting makes the stakeholder feel unheard. I then test the objection against the evidence, and if it is valid I change the proposal and say so. If it is not valid, I explain why with the evidence, and I offer a way to test the disagreement, such as a pilot or a review of the data.
questions.question: You are the BA in a review meeting where a stakeholder objects to every point you make, and the meeting is going nowhere. How do you handle it?

questions.answer: I start by understanding the new stakeholder's priorities and concerns, and I explain the project in terms of what matters to them. I ask what they need to decide and what would give them confidence, then I provide it. I also introduce them to the key team members, so they build their own relationships rather than relying on me as the only link.
questions.question: You are the BA and a new senior stakeholder joins the project halfway through, with no background and strong opinions about how it should run. How do you bring them up to speed and win their support?

questions.answer: I take each requirement and write the happy path first, then the failure cases: invalid data, missing data, boundary values, and system errors. I use the acceptance criteria as my checklist, so every criterion has at least one scenario. I then review the scenarios with the tester and the business user together, because each of them spots different gaps.
questions.question: You are the BA handed a set of payment requirements with no test scenarios. How do you turn the requirements into test scenarios the test team can actually use?

questions.answer: I agree the scope, the test data, the environment, and the entry and exit criteria with the business before testing starts. I prepare the test cases with the business users, using real examples from their daily work, and I agree who tests what and by when. I also plan for defect triage meetings, so issues are decided quickly rather than piling up.
questions.question: You are the BA asked to plan UAT for a new payment approval flow with 30 business users across three teams. How do you plan and coordinate it?

questions.answer: I explain the difference with the impact: severity is how badly the system is broken, such as a payment going to the wrong account, while priority is how urgently it must be fixed, such as a cosmetic error on a launch-critical screen. I triage with the business, the testers, and the developers together, agreeing both ratings for each defect. I record the reasons, so the same defect is not re-argued at every meeting.
questions.question: You are the BA in a defect triage meeting where the testers call a missing field 'critical' and the developers call it 'minor'. How do you resolve the severity versus priority argument?

questions.answer: I first check whether the field was genuinely missing from the requirements or whether it was implied and the tester expected it. If it was missing, I write the requirement with the business, assess the impact, and take it through change control. If it was implied, I clarify the requirement and ask the tester to retest. Either way I record the lesson, so the next requirements pack covers the field explicitly.
questions.question: You are the BA and a tester reports that a payment screen is missing a beneficiary reference field that was never in your requirements. Is it a defect, a missing requirement, or neither, and what do you do?

questions.answer: I identify the areas affected by the change, such as the payment types, the validations, and the downstream reports, and I select the existing test cases that cover them. I run those cases first, before any new tests, because a change to a shared validation can break a payment type nobody was thinking about. I also add a new test case for the change itself, so the regression pack grows with the system.
questions.question: You are the BA and a small change is made to the payment validation rules two days before go-live. How do you decide what regression testing is needed?

questions.answer: I walk the file from creation to settlement, checking each step: the file is created with the right format, the validations pass or fail as expected, the payments are processed, and the settlement and reporting match. I use a file with a mix of valid and invalid payments, so I can see both the successes and the rejections. I confirm the results with operations, who will run the file in production.
questions.question: You are the BA asked to test a payment file end to end before it goes live. What do you check at each stage, and how do you know the test passed?

questions.answer: I design negative cases around the most likely real mistakes: an invalid BIC, a currency the corridor does not support, a duplicate instruction, an amount over the limit, and a missing mandatory field. For each one I check that the system rejects the payment cleanly, shows a clear error, and does not partially process it. I also check that the rejected payment can be corrected and resubmitted without creating a duplicate.
questions.question: You are the BA writing negative test cases for a payment service. Which invalid inputs do you test first, and what should the system do with each one?

questions.answer: I use peak volumes from the busiest day, such as salary day or month-end, plus a margin for growth, and I test with those volumes end to end. I check not just whether the payments go through, but how long they take and whether any are lost or delayed. I also test what happens when the volume exceeds the target, so the team knows the breaking point before production finds it.
questions.question: You are the BA and the business says the new payment system must handle salary day, when volumes are ten times normal. How do you plan the performance and volume testing?

questions.answer: I use synthetic data that looks like real payments, with realistic names, amounts, and account details, but with no real customer information. I mask any real data that must be used, and I keep the test data separate from production. I also make sure the test data covers the edge cases, such as the largest and smallest amounts, and the currencies the system must support.
questions.question: You are the BA and the test team wants to use real customer payment data for testing, but compliance says no. How do you get test data that is realistic without using real customer details?

questions.answer: I agree the criteria before testing starts: all critical defects fixed, no open high-priority defects, the agreed test cases passed, and the business users confirming the system meets their needs. I track progress against those criteria in every status meeting, so sign-off is not a surprise. I also agree what happens to the defects that are deferred, with owners and dates, so sign-off does not mean the problems are forgotten.
questions.question: You are the BA and the business wants to sign off UAT, but three high-priority defects are still open. How do you decide whether the system is ready, and what do you tell the business?

questions.answer: I gather the evidence first: when the defect appeared, which payments were affected, and what changed recently. I work with the developers to find the root cause, whether it is a data issue, a rule change, or a system error. I then write the fix requirement with the root cause attached, and I add a test case that would have caught it, so the same defect does not return.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment defect appears in production a week after go-live, affecting 200 customers. How do you lead the root-cause investigation?

questions.answer: I check the requirement, the test case, and the test result for that specific scenario, to see whether the case was tested and what the result was. If the case was never written, the gap is in the requirements or the test design. If it was written but passed incorrectly, the gap is in the test data or the test execution. I fix the gap at its source and add the case to the regression pack.
questions.question: You are the BA and a defect reaches production that UAT should have caught. How do you find out why UAT missed it?

questions.answer: I ask the business users to test with their real daily work, not just the scripted cases, because they will try the combinations the test team never thought of. I also run a session where users attempt the unusual cases, such as correcting a payment after it was submitted, or handling a payment that arrives after cut-off. I record everything they find, even the small issues, and I triage them with the business.
questions.question: You are the BA and UAT is passing all its scripted cases, but you suspect the real users will still find problems on day one. What do you do?

questions.answer: I confirm the defect with a real example, then I assess its impact: how many payments, which customers, and what the business consequence is. I take it to the business with the options, such as fixing it before launch, launching with a workaround, or delaying the launch. I make sure the decision is recorded with its owner, so the team is not blamed later for a risk the business accepted.
questions.question: You are the BA in UAT and a tester finds that duplicate payments are sometimes created when a user double-clicks submit. How do you handle a defect found this late?

questions.answer: I use the requirements traceability to find every test case linked to the changed requirement, and I run those first. I then run the cases for the areas that share data or logic with the change, such as the payment validation and the reporting. I keep the regression pack updated with every release, so it reflects the current system rather than the system as it was a year ago.
questions.question: You are the BA and a change is made to how payment fees are calculated. How do you make sure the change has not broken anything else?

questions.answer: I check whether the test environment matches production: the same data, the same configuration, and the same interfaces. I then ask the tester to show me the exact steps and the result, and I compare it with the requirement. If the environment is the cause, I fix the environment and retest. If the requirement is unclear, I clarify it and update the document.
questions.question: You are the BA and a tester reports a defect that you cannot reproduce, but the tester insists it is real. How do you resolve the disagreement?

questions.answer: I agree the test data with the business and the testers before testing, using realistic examples that cover the main payment types and the edge cases. I make sure the data includes the failures as well as the successes, such as a payment with an invalid account number. I also check that the data is ready before the testers need it, so testing is not delayed by missing data.
questions.question: You are the BA and UAT is about to start, but the test data is not ready and the testers are waiting. What do you do?

questions.answer: I look at the defect's impact on the business, not just its technical severity: a defect that stops payments is critical, while a defect in a rarely used report is not. I ask the business to confirm the impact with real examples, and I agree the priority with the developers based on the effort to fix it. I then track the defect openly, so nobody is surprised by what is fixed and what is deferred.
questions.question: You are the BA in a triage meeting with 50 open defects and one week to go-live. How do you decide which defects must be fixed and which can wait?

questions.answer: I start by confirming the exact cut-off times and the value-date rules for each payment type, then I test payments submitted just before, at, and just after the cut-off. I check that the value date, the status, and the customer notification are all correct for each case. I also test what happens when a payment is submitted during a system outage, so the team knows whether it is queued, rejected, or lost.
questions.question: You are the BA testing a payment service where the value date depends on the cut-off time. How do you design test cases that prove the cut-off logic works?

questions.answer: I check the requirements, the test cases, and the test results for the changed area, and I compare them with the actual behaviour in production. I then work with the team to find whether the requirement was wrong, the test case was missing, or the test passed for the wrong reason. I write up the findings as lessons, and I add the missing test case to the regression pack.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment that passed all its tests in UAT fails in production for a customer in a new country. How do you investigate what went wrong?

questions.answer: I use the business's own examples, such as a payment that was returned by the beneficiary bank, and I write test cases for each return reason. I check that the system handles the return correctly: the payment status updates, the customer is notified, and the funds are returned to the right account. I also test that the original payment cannot be accidentally re-released when the return is processed.
questions.question: You are the BA testing how a payment system handles returns from the beneficiary bank. What test cases do you write, and what should happen in each one?

questions.answer: I ask the business to confirm the exact threshold, the approvers, and the action for each outcome, then I test amounts just below, at, and just above the threshold. I check that the approval workflow triggers correctly and that the payment cannot be released without the required approvals. I also test what happens when an approver rejects the payment, so the rejection path is verified as well as the approval path.
questions.question: You are the BA testing a payment approval rule where payments over a threshold need two approvers. How do you prove the rule works?

questions.answer: I agree the scope and the success criteria with the business before the pilot, and I select a small group of real users and real payments. I monitor the pilot daily, collecting defects and feedback, and I hold a review at the end to decide whether to proceed, fix, or roll back. I make sure the pilot users know they are testing, so they report problems instead of working around them.
questions.question: You are the BA and the business wants to pilot a new payment feature with a small group of customers before full launch. How do you plan the pilot as a test?

questions.answer: I check the requirement for the limit, the test data for the payment, and the system configuration, because the failure is usually in one of those three places. I then work with the developer to find whether the limit is being applied to the wrong amount, such as the gross amount instead of the net amount. I update the requirement or the test case with the correct interpretation, and I retest with amounts around the limit.
questions.question: You are the BA and a tester reports that a payment just over the daily limit was accepted when it should have been rejected. How do you investigate?

questions.answer: I ask the tester to show me the exact steps, the data, and the expected result from the requirement, then I run the same steps myself. If the behaviour differs from the requirement, it is a defect. If the requirement is silent on the case, I take it to the business to decide the correct behaviour. I record the decision and update the requirement, so the test is not argued again.
questions.question: You are the BA and a developer says a UAT defect is 'working as designed', but the tester says it contradicts the requirements. How do you decide who is right?

questions.answer: I start with the payments that are most at risk, such as the highest volumes, the largest amounts, and the most complex rules. I write test cases for each risk, and I agree the coverage with the business and the testers. I then track which cases have passed and which are still open, so the business can see the real state of testing rather than a percentage that hides the risky areas.
questions.question: You are the BA and the test team asks you which areas of a payment system need the most testing, but there is not enough time to test everything. How do you prioritise?

questions.answer: I check whether the requirement was written, whether the test case covered it, and whether the test environment matched production. I then find the first point where the chain broke, and I fix that link rather than blaming the tester. I add the missing case to the regression pack and I update the requirements, so the gap is closed for the next release.
questions.question: You are the BA and a production incident is traced to a requirement that was never tested. How do you find out why it was missed, and what do you change?

questions.answer: I use the production incident as the starting point: what happened, which payments were affected, and what the system should have done. I then write a test case that reproduces the incident, and I check that the fix resolves it. I also look for similar cases that could fail in the same way, and I add test cases for them too.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment fails in production because of a rare combination of currency and payment type. How do you make sure the fix is properly tested?

questions.answer: I agree the test approach with the business, including the scope, the data, and the sign-off criteria, before testing starts. I keep the business informed of progress and of any defects that affect their decision. At the end I present the results against the agreed criteria, with the open defects and their impact, so the business can make an informed sign-off decision.
questions.question: You are the BA coordinating UAT for a payment system where the business users are in different countries and have different working hours. How do you keep the testing on track?

questions.answer: I ask the business to define the expected behaviour for each error, such as an invalid account number or a missing currency, and I write test cases for each one. I check that the error message is clear, that the payment is not partially processed, and that the user can correct the error and resubmit. I also test that the error is logged, so operations can investigate it later.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment is rejected by the clearing system with an error code the business does not understand. How do you design tests that prove the error handling works?

questions.answer: I compare the test result with the requirement and the test data, and I ask the tester to show me the exact steps they followed. If the data is wrong, I fix the data and retest. If the requirement is ambiguous, I clarify it with the business. If the system is wrong, I raise a defect with the evidence, so the developer can reproduce it.
questions.question: You are the BA and a test fails, but nobody can agree whether the test data, the requirement, or the system is at fault. How do you find the cause?

questions.answer: I check the configuration, the data, and the code changes that went into the release, because a defect that appears after a release is usually caused by one of those. I then work with the team to reproduce the defect in the test environment, and I compare the behaviour with the previous release. I write the fix requirement with the cause attached, so the same mistake is not repeated.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment feature that worked in UAT stops working after the production release. How do you investigate?

questions.answer: I use the incident to write a test case that reproduces the exact failure, and I run it against the fix to prove the fix works. I then look for other cases that could fail in the same way, such as other payment types or other currencies, and I add test cases for them. I also update the regression pack, so the incident is covered in every future release.
questions.question: You are the BA and a duplicate payment is made in production because a retry was not handled correctly. How do you test the fix so you can be confident it will not happen again?

questions.answer: I ask the business to confirm the exact behaviour they expect when the downstream system is down: should payments be queued, rejected, or retried? I then write test cases for each scenario, including the recovery when the system comes back. I check that no payments are lost or duplicated during the outage, and that operations are alerted.
questions.question: You are the BA testing a payment service that depends on a downstream system that sometimes goes down. How do you test the outage scenarios?

questions.answer: I agree the entry criteria with the testers, such as the environment being ready and the test data being available, and the exit criteria, such as the defect targets being met. I track progress against those criteria daily, and I raise any blockers early. I do not let testing start before it is ready, because a false start wastes more time than a short delay.
questions.question: You are the BA and UAT is due to start tomorrow, but the test environment is not ready and the test data is incomplete. Do you start anyway, and what do you tell the business?

questions.answer: I check the test case against the requirement, and I ask the business to confirm the expected behaviour for the specific payment. If the test case is wrong, I correct it and retest. If the requirement is wrong, I update it through change control. I record the reason for the change, so the test history remains accurate.
questions.question: You are the BA and a test case fails, but the business says the system is actually behaving correctly and the test case is wrong. How do you handle it?

questions.answer: I use the requirements to write the test scenarios for the new corridor, including the currency, the cut-off times, and the local rules. I test with real examples from the new country, and I check that the payments settle correctly and the reporting is accurate. I also test the failure cases, such as an invalid local account format, so the corridor is ready for real customers.
questions.question: You are the BA and a new country corridor is being opened for payments. How do you plan the testing for a corridor that has never been used before?

questions.answer: I start by finding out what the business needs to know from the report: which payments, which time period, and which totals. I then test the report against the underlying payment data, checking that the totals match and that no payments are missing or double-counted. I also test the report with edge cases, such as a payment that was returned or corrected.
questions.question: You are the BA testing a new payment reconciliation report that the finance team will rely on for month-end. How do you prove the report is accurate?

questions.answer: I ask the tester to show me the steps and the result, and I compare them with the requirement and the test data. If the tester is right, I raise a defect with the evidence. If the developer is right, I ask the developer to explain the design and I update the requirement if it was unclear. I make sure the discussion is about the evidence, not about who is right.
questions.question: You are the BA in a meeting where a tester and a developer disagree about whether a payment behaviour is a defect. How do you resolve it without taking sides?

questions.answer: I gather the evidence: the requirement, the test result, and the production incident, and I present them to the team. I then lead a discussion on what should change: the requirement, the test case, or the process that allowed the gap. I record the agreed actions with owners and dates, so the lesson is acted on rather than just discussed.
questions.question: You are the BA asked to run a lessons-learned session after a payment defect reached production. How do you run it so the team actually changes something?

questions.answer: I design the API around the business action, such as creating a payment instruction, with a clear resource, a unique reference, and the fields the business needs. I include the idempotency key, the validation rules, and the error responses in the design, and I agree the contract with the consumers before building. I also version the API from the start, so future changes do not break existing consumers.
questions.question: You are the BA designing a REST API for creating payment instructions, and three different teams will consume it. How do you design the API so it works for all of them?

questions.answer: I require the client to send a unique idempotency key with each payment request, and I make the system store the key with the payment's result. If the same key arrives again, the system returns the original result instead of creating a second payment. I also test the retry scenario explicitly, so a network timeout cannot turn one payment into two.
questions.question: You are the BA and a client retries a payment request after a network timeout, and the customer is paid twice. How do you design idempotency into the API to prevent this?

questions.answer: I use webhooks when the consumer needs to know immediately, such as when a payment status changes, and the consumer can receive and acknowledge the event. I use polling when the consumer cannot receive webhooks, or when the updates are infrequent and the consumer can check on a schedule. I document the choice with its trade-offs, including what happens if a webhook is missed or a poll is delayed.
questions.question: You are the BA choosing between webhooks and polling for payment status updates to a corporate client. How do you decide, and what are the risks of each?

questions.answer: I define the error codes with the business and the developers, distinguishing between errors the client can fix, such as invalid data, and errors the system must handle, such as a temporary outage. I agree the retry rules: which errors are retried, how many times, and with what delay, and I make sure retries use the same idempotency key. I also agree how errors are logged and reported, so operations can act on them.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment API returns a generic error when a payment fails, so the client cannot tell whether to retry or correct the data. How do you fix the error handling?

questions.answer: I start with the sensitivity of the data and the trust between the systems: OAuth is right when the API acts on behalf of a user, API keys are enough for simple system-to-system calls, and mTLS is needed when both sides must prove their identity. I check what the consumers already support and what the security team requires. I document the choice with its risks, and I make sure the authentication is tested, including the failure cases.
questions.question: You are the BA choosing authentication for a new payment API, and the security team wants mTLS while the client wants simple API keys. How do you decide what is appropriate?

questions.answer: I version the API from the first release, using a version in the URL or the header, and I agree the rules for breaking changes with the consumers. When a change is needed, I introduce the new version alongside the old one, give consumers a migration period, and announce the retirement date for the old version. I never change the meaning of an existing field in place, because that silently breaks every consumer.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment API needs a breaking change to a field, but five clients already use the current version. How do you manage the versioning and the migration?

questions.answer: I map the data and the rules between the two systems, starting with the payment types, the fields, and the validations. I find the gaps where the core system cannot support what the business needs, and I agree whether to change the process, the core system, or the integration. I also plan for the failure cases, such as the core system being unavailable, so payments are not lost.
questions.question: You are the BA integrating a new payment front end with a core banking system that was built twenty years ago. How do you approach the integration requirements?

questions.answer: I compare the two on the business needs: a file is right for bulk payments on a schedule, while an API is right for real-time, single payments that need an immediate response. I look at the volume, the timing, the error handling, and the cost of each option. I present the trade-offs to the business, because the choice affects how quickly payments are processed and how errors are handled.
questions.question: You are the BA and a corporate client asks whether to send payments by host-to-host file or by API. How do you help them choose?

questions.answer: I agree the behaviour with the business first: should payments be queued, rejected, or held for manual review when the downstream system is down? I then write the requirements for the queue, the retry logic, and the alerts, so operations know what is happening. I also test the recovery, so when the system comes back the queued payments are processed in the right order without duplicates.
questions.question: You are the BA and the downstream settlement system goes down for two hours, but payments keep arriving. What should the system do with them, and how do you write that requirement?

questions.answer: I list every field in both systems with its format, its meaning, and its transformation rule, and I test the mapping with real examples. I include the rules for missing or invalid data, and I agree what happens in each case. I also check that the mapped data can be reversed, so a payment can be traced back to its source.
questions.question: You are the BA mapping data between a payment system and a general ledger, and you find the two systems use different codes for the same payment type. How do you resolve the mapping?

questions.answer: I ask the business what 'real-time' means for them: is it seconds, minutes, or just faster than the current batch? I then check whether the downstream systems can support the required speed, and what happens if they cannot. I write the requirement with a measurable target and a fallback, so the team knows what to build and what to do when the target cannot be met.
questions.question: You are the BA and the business wants 'real-time' payment status updates, but the downstream system only updates every hour. How do you handle the gap between the ask and the reality?

questions.answer: I define the timeout, the retry count, and the delay between retries with the developers and the business, based on how long the downstream system normally takes. I make sure the retry uses the same idempotency key, so a retry cannot create a duplicate. I also agree what happens after the final retry fails, such as alerting operations and queuing the payment for manual review.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment API call times out, but the payment may or may not have been processed. How do you design the retry and the reconciliation so the payment is neither lost nor duplicated?

questions.answer: I check the API contract, the test cases, and the production logs to find where the behaviour diverges from the contract. I then work with the developer and the consumer to agree the correct behaviour, and I update the contract if it was unclear. I also add a test case for the specific scenario, so the same misunderstanding does not happen again.
questions.question: You are the BA and a client says your payment API is returning the wrong status, but your team says the API is working as designed. How do you resolve the dispute?

questions.answer: I start by understanding the business need: how quickly must the data be available, and what decisions depend on it? I then design the integration to meet that need, whether it is real-time, near-real-time, or batch. I include the error handling and the reconciliation, so the team knows when the data is wrong and how to fix it.
questions.question: You are the BA and the finance team needs payment data in the reporting system within an hour, but the current integration runs overnight. How do you design a faster integration without breaking the existing one?

questions.answer: I ask the business to define the priority: which payments must go first, and what happens to the rest? I then design a queue with clear rules, such as processing high-value payments first or processing in the order received. I write the requirements for the queue, the monitoring, and the alerts, so operations can see the backlog and act on it.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment API is receiving more requests than it can handle at peak times. How do you design the throttling and queuing so no payment is lost?

questions.answer: I agree the contract with the consumer, including the fields, the validations, and the error responses, before either side builds. I then test the integration with real examples, including the failure cases, and I agree a process for changing the contract. I also set up monitoring, so if the consumer sends invalid data, the team knows quickly.
questions.question: You are the BA integrating with a third-party payment provider whose API documentation is incomplete and whose support is slow. How do you get the integration built and tested?

questions.answer: I check the security requirements with the security team, including the encryption, the authentication, and the data retention. I then write the requirements for each of those, with the specific standards that must be met. I also agree how the security will be tested, including the failure cases such as an expired certificate or an invalid token.
questions.question: You are the BA and a new payment integration must meet strict security requirements, but the developers want to move fast and skip the security review. How do you handle the tension?

questions.answer: I map the end-to-end flow, including the systems, the messages, and the data at each step, and I find where the delay or the failure occurs. I then work with the teams that own each system to agree the fix, whether it is a data change, a rule change, or a system change. I write the fix requirement with the evidence, so the team can see why the change is needed.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment takes three days to settle, but the business promised customers one day. How do you find the bottleneck across five different systems?

questions.answer: I ask the business to confirm the exact rules for the new payment type, including the fields, the validations, and the settlement. I then check whether the existing API can support the new type, or whether a new version is needed. I write the requirements for the new type, and I test it with real examples before it goes live.
questions.question: You are the BA and the business wants to add a new payment type to an existing API, but the API was not designed for it. How do you decide whether to extend the API or build a new one?

questions.answer: I define the monitoring with operations, including what to watch, such as the error rate, the response time, and the queue length, and what to do when a threshold is breached. I agree the alerts, the owners, and the escalation path, so a problem is acted on quickly. I also agree what information the alerts must contain, so the person who receives the alert can act without having to investigate from scratch.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment API goes live, but nobody is monitoring it and failures are only discovered when customers complain. How do you set up the monitoring and alerting?

questions.answer: I start by confirming the facts: the payment reference, the amount, the value date, and the status at each stage of the journey. I then trace the payment through each system, checking where it stopped and why, and I keep the client updated with what I know and what I am checking next. Once I find the cause, I agree the fix, the timeline, and the compensation if any, and I record the lessons so the same failure is prevented.
questions.question: You are the BA on a case where a corporate client reports a high-value payment never arrived, but your system shows it as sent. Walk through how you investigate, what you tell the client, and how you prevent it happening again.

questions.answer: I start by defining the minimum viable product: which payment types, which customers, and which corridors must be ready on day one. I then sequence the work so the regulatory and core payment flows are built first, with the enhancements in later releases. I agree the plan with the business and the technology teams, and I track the risks weekly, so the launch date is based on evidence rather than hope.
questions.question: You are the BA on a project to launch a new real-time payment product in three months, but the team says six months is realistic. How do you plan a launch that is both fast and safe?

questions.answer: I gather the evidence the regulator needs: the screening rules, the test results, and the audit trail for the payments in question. I check that the evidence is complete and accurate, and I present it with a clear explanation of how the screening works. I also identify any gaps and agree a plan to close them, so the regulator sees a controlled process rather than a scramble.
questions.question: You are the BA and a regulator asks for evidence that your sanctions screening is working correctly. How do you prepare the response, and what do you do if you find a gap?

questions.answer: I first find out why the migration is behind: is it the data, the testing, or the dependencies on other teams? I then replan with the team, focusing on the critical path and the items that can be deferred. I tell the sponsor the truth about the new date, with the options and their costs, and I agree a recovery plan with clear milestones.
questions.question: You are the BA on a payments migration that is three weeks behind schedule with a fixed go-live date. How do you recover, and what do you tell the sponsor?

questions.answer: I stop further payments immediately and confirm the scale: how many customers, how much money, and which payments were duplicated. I then work with finance and operations to agree the recovery: reversing the duplicates, contacting the customers, and fixing the root cause. I also write an incident summary that explains what happened, why, and what will change, so the business and the customers are informed.
questions.question: You are the BA and a duplicate payment run has paid 500 customers twice. What do you do in the first hour, the first day, and the first week?

questions.answer: I start by understanding the new corridor: the currency, the local rules, the cut-off times, and the settlement arrangements. I then map the end-to-end flow, including the systems, the messages, and the data, and I identify the gaps. I agree the requirements with the business and the technology teams, and I plan the testing with real examples from the new country.
questions.question: You are the BA asked to open a new country corridor for payments, but nobody in the team has worked with that country before. How do you approach it?

questions.answer: I gather the data first: when the spike started, which feature changed, and which payments are affected. I then work with the fraud team to understand the pattern, and I agree a short-term fix, such as tightening a control or rolling back the feature. I write the requirements for the longer-term fix, and I make sure the change is tested before it goes live.
questions.question: You are the BA and a fraud spike appears the week after a new payment feature launches. How do you investigate, and what do you recommend?

questions.answer: I define the success criteria for the pilot, including the volumes, the customer feedback, and the defect targets. I select a small group of customers and monitor the pilot daily, collecting feedback and defects. At the end I present the results to the business with a recommendation: proceed, fix and retry, or stop, based on the evidence.
questions.question: You are the BA and the business wants to pilot a new payment service with 100 customers before a full launch. How do you design the pilot so the results are meaningful?

questions.answer: I start by confirming the regulatory requirement and the deadline, then I work backwards to the requirements that must be delivered. I separate the items that are legally required from the items that are good practice, and I sequence the work so the legal minimum is ready first. I keep the sponsor informed of the trade-offs, so the decision to defer anything is explicit.
questions.question: You are the BA on a project where a new regulation requires additional checks on all cross-border payments, but the deadline is in eight weeks and the full solution will take twelve. What do you do?

questions.answer: I ask the business to show me the complaints and the payment examples, then I trace them through the process to find the common cause. I present the findings with the evidence, and I propose a fix that addresses the root cause, not just the symptoms. I agree the fix with the business and I define how its success will be measured.
questions.question: You are the BA and customers keep complaining that their payments are delayed, but each complaint sounds different. How do you find the real cause and propose a fix?

questions.answer: I bring the two teams together with the shared goal, such as getting payments to customers on time, and I ask each team to explain its requirement and its reason. I look for a compromise, such as different treatment for different payment types, or a phased approach. If no compromise exists, I escalate with the options and a recommendation, and I record the decision.
questions.question: You are the BA in a project where operations and compliance cannot agree on a payment approval flow, and the launch date is at risk. How do you resolve the deadlock?

questions.answer: I first confirm the impact: which payments are affected, how many customers, and what the business consequence is. I then work with the technology team to understand the cause and the fix, and I keep the business updated with the progress. I write an incident summary that explains what happened, what was done, and what will change, so the business can inform its customers.
questions.question: You are the BA and a production payment system fails on salary day, when volumes are at their highest. How do you manage the incident and the communication?

questions.answer: I start by understanding the new payment type: the rules, the fields, and the settlement arrangements. I then map the end-to-end flow and identify the gaps in the current system. I agree the requirements with the business and the technology teams, and I plan the testing with real examples, including the failure cases.
questions.question: You are the BA asked to design the requirements for a new instant payment service that must settle in seconds, but the current system settles overnight. How do you approach the design?

questions.answer: I gather the evidence: the payment details, the system logs, and the audit trail, and I present them to the regulator with a clear explanation. I also identify the root cause and the fix, and I agree a plan to prevent a recurrence. I keep the communication factual and timely, so the regulator sees a controlled response.
questions.question: You are the BA and a regulator asks why a sanctioned payment was released. How do you investigate and respond?

questions.answer: I ask the vendor for the details of the change, the impact, and the timeline, then I assess the effect on our payments, our testing, and our launch date. I present the options to the business, such as accepting the change, delaying the launch, or finding a workaround. I agree the plan with the business and I update the requirements and the test pack.
questions.question: You are the BA and a key payment vendor announces a breaking change to their API with only four weeks' notice. How do you manage the impact?

questions.answer: I start by defining the minimum viable product for the new segment, using the existing payment types and the simplest flow that meets the segment's needs. I then agree the requirements with the business, focusing on what is different for the new segment rather than rebuilding everything. I plan the testing with real examples from the new segment, and I agree the launch criteria.
questions.question: You are the BA and the business wants to launch payments for a new customer segment, but the current system was built for a different segment. How do you adapt the requirements?

questions.answer: I find out why the project is failing: is it the scope, the team, the technology, or the business support? I then present the findings to the sponsor with the options: fix the root cause and continue, reduce the scope and relaunch, or stop the project. I make sure the decision is based on evidence, not on sunk cost, and I record the reasons.
questions.question: You are the BA on a payments project that has missed three deadlines and the sponsor is considering cancelling it. How do you assess whether it can be saved?

questions.answer: I ask the business to define the expected behaviour for each error, and I write test cases that prove the system handles each one correctly. I check that the error is logged, that the customer is informed, and that the payment can be corrected and resubmitted. I also test the recovery, so when the system comes back, the queued payments are processed without duplicates.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment system must handle a downstream outage without losing or duplicating payments. How do you design and test the outage handling?

questions.answer: I start by understanding the business need for the new feature, then I map the end-to-end flow and identify the systems and the data involved. I agree the requirements with the business and the technology teams, and I plan the testing with real examples. I also agree the rollout plan, including the pilot and the rollback, so the launch is controlled.
questions.question: You are the BA asked to lead the requirements for a new payment feature that will be used by 10,000 corporate customers. How do you plan the work from elicitation to launch?

questions.answer: I gather the facts: which payments were affected, what the system did, and what it should have done. I then work with the team to find the root cause, and I agree the fix and the testing. I write the incident summary with the timeline, the impact, and the lessons, and I present it to the business with the actions and the owners, so the incident leads to real change.
questions.question: You are the BA and a payment incident affects 1,000 customers. The business wants an incident summary by the end of the day. How do you write it, and what do you include?
